title: Financial Examiners
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For financial examiners broadly, the emergence of systemic risks from advanced AI models [7][17] and the proposal of rules for prediction markets [5] require updated methods for reviewing and analyzing new laws to determine their impact [O*NET Task 12] and establishing guidelines for implementation [O*NET Task 11]. The regulatory mandate that banks cannot outsource judgment to algorithms [16] shifts the investigation of activities [O*NET Task 5] and the review of audit reports [O*NET Task 8] toward the verification of continuous human supervisory oversight. For a subset of workers in consumer lending, the movement to narrow civil rights protections [1] may alter how examiners recommend actions to ensure compliance [O*NET Task 2] by reducing the weight of certain disparate impact metrics. For examiners in AI governance subsegments, the proposal for audit-ready controls [2] shifts the evaluation of data processing applications [O*NET Task 14] toward the verification of automated control logs. For examiners in the infrastructure subsegment, monitoring new data center accounting trends [3] alters the review of balance sheets and loan documentation [O*NET Task 6] to account for specialized asset valuations. For examiners in regions utilizing "live testing" cohorts for AI, as reported in the United Kingdom [8], the investigation of activities [O*NET Task 5] moves toward active, real-time oversight. For examiners in regions implementing digital asset frameworks, as reported in the European Union [9], the MiCA regulation increases the volume of registration reviews [O*NET Task 15]. In those same regions, as reported in the European Union [13], the rise of AI-accelerated cyber threats shifts the investigation of activities [O*NET Task 5] to include the technical oversight of critical tech providers, while the adoption of digital currency standards [15] requires the evaluation of data processing applications [O*NET Task 14] to integrate new technical payment standards. For examiners in regions conducting risk assessments for specific AI models, as reported in Japan [10], the evaluation of data processing applications [O*NET Task 14] now includes analyzing the operational risk of specific model deployments. For examiners in regions where legislation establishes federal registration pathways for non-bank payment providers, as reported in the United States [11][14], the review of applications for acceptance [O*NET Task 15] expands to include non-bank FinTech entities. Verifying and inspecting cash reserves and assigned collateral [O*NET Task 16] is unlikely to change because objective, third-party physical verification remains a binding requirement for solvency confirmation.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, examiners broadly will integrate AI-specific risk criteria and human-oversight mandates into their workflows, while practitioners in specific regional jurisdictions will adapt to real-time AI oversight and expanded registration reviews for non-bank FinTechs.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For financial examiners in the AI governance and digital asset subsegments, if current trajectories hold, the nature of compliance verification may shift. Extrapolating from the push for audit-ready AI controls [2] and "regulator-in-the-loop" strategies [4], the process of investigating activities to ensure legality [O*NET Task 5] may transition from manual transaction sampling toward the validation of automated governance logs and real-time data streams. In the consumer lending subsegment, the specific actions recommended to ensure compliance [O*NET Task 2] could become increasingly dependent on the forensic analysis of algorithmic decision-logs to detect subtle shifts in lending patterns. Despite these shifts, direct and participating in formal meetings with bank directors and senior management [O*NET Task 1] is unlikely to change because the resolution of "questionable financial conditions" requires high-stakes human negotiation and the assessment of management's qualitative judgment.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, examiners in AI and digital asset subsegments may shift from periodic sampling to the continuous validation of automated governance streams.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For examiners in AI governance subsegments, the ability to provide effective oversight depends on whether regulators close the technical gap between their capabilities and those of the banks they oversee [17]. One outcome involves the adoption of regulatory AI that can autonomously monitor bank models in real-time, shifting the investigation of activities [O*NET Task 5] to a meta-review of the regulatory AI's performance. A rival outcome exists where regulatory lag persists, shifting the occupation toward retrospective forensic auditing, where examiners primarily investigate AI-driven systemic failures after they occur. A significant unknown remains whether the legal definition of "judgment" [16] can be codified into a computable standard or if it remains an irreducible human requirement. The preparation of reports and exhibits detailing an institution's safety and soundness [O*NET Task 3] will likely resist full automation because these documents serve as legal records of accountability that require a human signatory.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, examiners in AI subsegments may transition to managing autonomous regulatory AI that monitors bank-level models in real-time.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, examiners in AI subsegments may shift toward a purely forensic role, auditing the failures of complex models that have surpassed the capacity for proactive oversight.*

title: Credit Counselors
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For credit counselors broadly, the prevalence of negative equity in vehicle loans [1] may increase the complexity of prioritizing client debt repayment and recommending strategies for debt resolution [2]. Because a significant portion of drivers owe more than their vehicles are worth, counselors may need to adjust spending plans to account for assets that cannot be easily liquidated to reduce debt [2]. This market condition could increase the frequency of negotiating with creditors to prevent repossessions for clients who are unable to trade in underwater vehicles [2]. However, the core mechanism of calculating clients' available monthly income is unlikely to change, as the basic arithmetic of cash flow remains independent of asset equity [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, credit counselors may focus more heavily on vehicle-specific debt restructuring to address rising negative equity among consumers.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For credit counselors broadly, if current trajectories of asset devaluation hold, counselors may face a persistent requirement to integrate asset-depreciation modeling into estimating time for debt repayment [1][2]. Extrapolating from current vehicle trends, explaining general financial topics may shift toward educating clients on the systemic risks of negative equity across various loan types [2]. This shift could lead to more specialized debt management plans that prioritize the stabilization of underwater assets to avoid catastrophic financial collapse [2]. Despite these shifts, interviewing clients in person or by phone is likely to persist, as the psychological distress associated with severe debt often requires human empathy and active listening to ensure client compliance [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, if negative equity patterns persist, credit counselors may integrate more complex asset-depreciation modeling into their debt management plans.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For credit counselors broadly, the long-term evolution of the role remains uncertain and depends on whether lending structures are fundamentally reformed to prevent negative equity. One plausible outcome is that the role shifts toward high-level strategic negotiation, as automated systems handle the routine reviewing of changes to financial situations by monitoring asset values in real-time [2]. Alternatively, if systemic shifts toward subscription-based ownership or stricter lending mandates eliminate negative equity, the role may return to a primary focus on general financial literacy and budgeting [2]. Maintaining or updating records of client account activity will likely resist change due to the enduring legal requirements of debt contracts and regulatory auditing [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the role may shift toward high-level strategic negotiation as automated systems handle the routine monitoring of asset equity.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the role may return to general financial literacy and budgeting if structural lending reforms eliminate the possibility of negative equity.*

title: Loan Officers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For the occupation broadly, current shifts are driven by a combination of regulatory constraints and evolving borrower behaviors, while specific subsegments experience targeted automation. Loan officers must increasingly manage borrower hesitation and market misconceptions when they meet with applicants to obtain information [7]. For the occupation broadly, the implementation of the CFPB final rule on the Equal Credit Opportunity Act maintains provisions regarding disparate impact, which constrains the mechanism used to analyze applicants' financial status to ensure non-discriminatory outcomes [11]. In organizations utilizing advanced LLM integrations for commercial banking, the tasks of document collection and the initial lending lifecycle are being handed off to artificial intelligence [15]. For a subset of workers in mortgage lending, the adoption of "verification-first" models may shift the task of analyzing applicants' financial status toward raw income verification rather than reliance on traditional debt-to-income ratios [4]. In the auto-lending subsegment, the prevalence of negative equity in vehicle assets may alter how loan officers analyze financial status to account for underwater collateral [14]. For small-volume lenders, streamlined credit report access may reduce the manual effort required to obtain and compile copies of loan applicants' credit histories [5]. The task of approving loans outside specified limits is unlikely to change yet because institutional risk thresholds and senior-level fiduciary accountability remain centralized [10].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, AI agents and streamlined data access will reduce the administrative burden of data gathering for a subset of loan officers, while the broader occupation will focus more on navigating regulatory constraints and managing borrower sentiment during the application process.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For a subset of workers in organizations adopting agentic AI, if current trajectories in borrower-side AI agency hold, the task of meeting with applicants to obtain information may shift toward managing data exchanges between competing agentic systems [6]. Extrapolating from the development of compliance-trusted AI, the task of reviewing loan agreements to ensure accuracy could shift from manual file review toward auditing AI-generated compliance reports [10]. In mortgage-specific contexts, if verification-first income analysis becomes standardized, human labor may concentrate on the task of conferring with underwriters to resolve complex application problems that require high-level negotiation or exception handling [4]. The task of handling customer complaints is likely to persist as a human-led activity because the social perceptiveness required to resolve interpersonal disputes and emotional volatility is not currently replicated by agentic architectures.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, for those in integrated settings, the verification and review of loan files may become largely automated, shifting the human role toward managing complex exceptions and interpersonal disputes.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For loan officers in highly integrated AI environments, the distribution of decision authority remains unknown. If AI systems achieve high-fidelity predictive accuracy for risk, the task of approving loans within specified limits may shift entirely to algorithmic execution, leaving humans to manage only the most anomalous cases. Conversely, if regulatory regimes increase the cost of "black box" decisions, human loan officers may be required to provide a narrated justification for every approval to satisfy audit requirements. The task of working with clients to identify financial goals may resist full automation even at this horizon because of the high error cost associated with misaligning long-term financial strategy with personal life constraints.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the role may evolve into a purely auditing function, where humans oversee the systemic health of automated lending portfolios.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the role may bifurcate into a high-touch, human-centric advisory service for complex assets, while standard credit is entirely commoditized and automated.*

title: Tax Examiners and Collectors, and Revenue Agents
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For agents in national revenue agencies, such as the UK's HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) and the US Internal Revenue Service (IRS), the mechanism for executing administrative communication is shifting toward AI-assisted workflows. In the United Kingdom, the deployment of AI copilots to thousands of staff facilitates the automation of drafting for tasks to send notices to taxpayers when accounts are delinquent and to contact taxpayers by mail or telephone [7]. For a subset of workers managing large business customers in the UK, updated guidance modifies the process for examining and analyzing tax assets and liabilities to manage compliance risk [9]. In the United States, the operational capacity to enter tax return information into computers for processing may remain dependent on the availability of supplemental legislative funding, such as the Inflation Reduction Act [2]. For agents in the UK, the process for reviewing filed tax returns to determine whether claimed tax credits and deductions are allowed by law is governed by a system of detailed administrative manuals covering employment income, minimum wage, and employment-related securities [3][4][6]. Specifically, for agents in Northern Ireland, new regulations modify the mechanism for reviewing filed tax returns concerning customs duty repayments [5], while specific rules for further education institutions alter the process for auditing VAT liability [8]. In jurisdictions where prediction markets are legally contested, as reported in New Hampshire and other US states, the requirement to maintain knowledge of tax code changes increases to incorporate new taxable wagering structures [1]. The authority to direct service of legal documents, such as subpoenas or warrants, is unlikely to change because this function is derived from statutory legal mandates rather than administrative software.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, agents in specific national agencies may see a reduction in time spent on clerical drafting, while their operational capacity remains sensitive to supplemental funding and the introduction of new taxable digital asset classes.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For revenue agencies that have integrated AI-assisted drafting and those subject to periodic funding appropriations, if current trajectories hold, the reduction in time spent on clerical tasks may allow agents to increase the frequency of the task to confer with taxpayers or their representatives to resolve problems with returns [7]. Extrapolating from funding patterns in the United States, the capacity to review selected tax returns to determine the nature of audits may remain conditional on periodic appropriation cycles rather than permanent structural funding [2]. In jurisdictions where prediction markets are codified, agents may shift more focus toward the task to examine accounting systems and records to verify that digital platform computations comply with statutory provisions [1]. The requirement to participate in informal appeals hearings on contested cases persists unchanged because these proceedings require human judgment to navigate adversarial interpersonal dynamics [3].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the role of agents in AI-adopting agencies could shift toward more complex taxpayer negotiations, although audit capacity may remain volatile due to funding dependencies.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For revenue agencies with established AI-augmented workflows, the long-term structural evolution depends on whether AI tools move from drafting to the autonomous analysis of sensitive financial data. One plausible outcome is that agents utilize advanced models to determine appropriate methods of debt settlement by analyzing patterns in financial records to identify the most effective seizure or settlement mechanism [7]. A competing outcome is that strict privacy constraints and regulatory barriers prevent the delegation of liability determination to AI, keeping the technology limited to the summarization of records. It remains unknown whether the legal authority to secure a taxpayer's agreement to discharge a tax assessment will remain an exclusively human function. The requirement to maintain records for each case, including contacts and actions taken, will resist change as it remains a fundamental requirement for legal audit trails and judicial review.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, AI may move from administrative support to suggesting specific debt settlement methods based on autonomous financial pattern analysis.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, regulatory and privacy constraints may restrict AI to clerical drafting, maintaining the human agent as the sole determinant of tax liability.*

title: Tax Preparers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For tax preparers broadly, the deployment of AI agents capable of drafting tax returns [3][4] shifts the task of preparing simple to complex tax returns [5] from manual composition to the verification of machine-generated drafts. For tax preparers in the United Kingdom, the use of specific government guidance for National Insurance contributions and Construction Industry Scheme refunds [1][2] means the task of computing taxes owed or overpaid [1] is increasingly executed via standardized digital logic provided by the state. In the same region, requirements for reporting payrolled car benefits to the state [6] modify the task of reviewing financial records to determine forms needed [6], necessitating adherence to specific electronic reporting formats. For tax preparers in India, the integration of AI agents into filing platforms [5] may shift the task of interviewing clients to obtain taxable income and deductible expenses [4] toward asynchronous, AI-mediated data collection. The task of explaining federal and state tax laws to individuals and companies [8] is unlikely to change in the near term because the high error cost of legal misinterpretation requires a licensed professional to provide final interpretive authority.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, tax preparers will transition from primary drafters to editors of AI-generated returns, while those in digitally integrated jurisdictions will rely on state-provided logic for specific liability computations.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For tax preparers broadly, if the adoption of AI drafting agents continues, the task of reviewing financial records to determine forms needed [6] may shift toward an audit-style verification of AI-categorized financial data. For preparers in regions with integrated digital tax infrastructure, the task of consulting tax law handbooks or bulletins for atypical returns [10] may be reduced for standardized schemes as the logic is embedded directly into the drafting tools [1][2]. However, the task of checking data input or verifying totals to detect errors [7] persists because the legal liability for the accuracy of the filing remains with the human preparer. The requirement to furnish taxpayers with sufficient information and advice to ensure correct completion [3] remains necessary to manage the risk boundary between aggressive tax minimization and non-compliance.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the core value of the tax preparer shifts from the technical execution of return preparation to the legal certification and risk management of automated outputs.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For tax preparers broadly, the possibility of real-time state-led data reconciliation introduces rival outcomes. If governments implement systems where credits and deductions are applied automatically at the point of transaction, the task of preparing simple tax returns [5] and claiming specific refunds [1] may be eliminated. Conversely, if financial instruments and corporate layering increase in complexity, the task of reviewing financial records to determine forms [6] may resist further automation. It remains unknown whether state-led automation will encompass all atypical returns or if a permanent niche for high-complexity manual synthesis will persist. Even at this horizon, the task of calculating form preparation fees according to complexity [11] remains a business-level pricing decision resistant to technical automation.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, real-time government reconciliation and AI drafting eliminate the need for human intervention in the majority of individual and small business tax filings.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, increasing complexity in global financial instruments and corporate layering preserves the necessity for human preparers to manually synthesize records and trigger complex claims.*

title: Financial Quantitative Analysts
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For quantitative analysts broadly, the adoption of AI-assisted coding, or "vibe coding," may accelerate the research and development of analytical tools [O*NET 2] and the testing of new analytical software [O*NET 10] by reducing the friction between prototype and production [4]. For a subset of analysts in AI-first hedge funds, the deployment of AI to make autonomous trade selections may shift how mathematical techniques are applied to securities trading [O*NET 1] [3]. In regulated prediction markets, the task of defining model specifications [O*NET 5] will likely be constrained by new frameworks established by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) [2]. In organizations using AI-integrated financial terminals, the process of providing analytical support to researchers [O*NET 8] may shift as chatbot-style interfaces change how complex datasets are queried and extracted [5]. In high-stakes AI-first settings, the human role in maintaining financial analytic models [O*NET 7] serves as a critical safeguard, as human judgment acts as a "moat" to prevent catastrophic errors that autonomous systems might overlook [1]. The task of producing written summary reports [O*NET 6] is unlikely to change significantly yet, as these documents provide the essential audit trail for regulatory accountability.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, the occupation will see a bifurcated shift: a broad acceleration in model prototyping via AI-assisted coding, and a specialized requirement for analysts in AI-first or highly regulated settings to align autonomous agents with emerging regulatory mandates and data interfaces.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For a subset of analysts in AI-first and regulated settings, the role may shift toward the formal auditing of AI-generated tools if current trajectories in autonomous agent deployment hold [3]. Extrapolating from the move toward structured AI prediction market rules [2], the task of devising independent models to verify results [O*NET 9] could evolve into a primary regulatory and compliance function to ensure autonomous systems remain within legal and risk bounds [2]. The fundamental requirement for applying mathematical or statistical techniques [O*NET 1] will persist unchanged, as these provide the only objective basis for validating the outputs of autonomous analytical tools against actual market performance.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, for the subsegment of analysts in AI-driven environments, the occupational focus may pivot from primary model construction toward the regulatory verification and auditing of autonomous quantitative tools.*

## Far (2046–2051)

Within regulated AI-first financial contexts, the role of the analyst may diverge based on the maturity of automated oversight [1][3]. One possibility is that analysts evolve into systemic architects who focus on the high-level task of defining model specifications [O*NET 5] for fleets of autonomous systems, emphasizing structural integrity and systemic risk [1]. A rival outcome is that the standardization of AI regulatory protocols [2] commoditizes the "human moat," reducing the specialized value of the individual model builder. It remains unknown whether regulatory bodies will ever permit the fully autonomous valuation of complex instruments without a legally accountable human signatory. The fundamental task of interpreting results of financial analysis procedures [O*NET 3] will likely resist change, as fiduciary responsibility for catastrophic loss requires a human agent.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, analysts in this subsegment may evolve into system architects who govern and certify the behavior of autonomous quantitative model fleets.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the standardization of AI regulatory audits may erode the specialized value of the human builder, commoditizing the task of model development.*

title: Fraud Examiners, Investigators and Analysts
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For fraud examiners broadly, the proliferation of frontier AI in adversarial contexts may alter the task of researching or evaluating new technologies for use in fraud detection systems [7]. Because synthetic corporate identities can be fabricated to mimic legitimate firms, the task of gathering financial documents related to investigations can no longer assume the authenticity of registered corporate entities [1]. In billion-dollar firms, analyzing financial data to detect irregularities shifts toward identifying agent-driven identity threats and synthetic patterns [9]. For a subset of workers managing agentic commerce and automated expense systems, analyzing financial data shifts from monitoring human behavioral patterns to identifying agent-hijacking or automated expense anomalies [4][6][23]. In organizations adopting AI-driven continuous monitoring, the task of reviewing reports of suspected fraud could shift from one-by-one incident review toward automated triage and high-scale error detection [11][16]. For a subsegment of examiners in the financial sector, the task of interviewing witnesses or suspects is challenged by deepfakes and shadow AI, necessitating new biometric or cryptographic authentication protocols [13][14][15]. In regions where attackers utilize search result manipulation to redirect payments, reviewing reports of suspected fraud shifts toward analyzing external digital redirects and poisoned search results [3]. For a subsegment of examiners in the banking sector, coordinating investigative efforts may shift toward the use of inter-bank shared datasets and real-time confirmation tools to verify payment authenticity [10][18]. For a subsegment of examiners in online marketplaces, evaluating business operations to identify risk areas expands from detecting counterfeit goods to analyzing behavioral trust issues and seller manipulation [12][21]. For examiners specializing in prediction markets, evaluating business operations to identify risk areas may expand to include the physical manipulation of environmental sensors to rig outcome-based bets [17]. For fraud examiners broadly, interviewing witnesses or suspects may now require identifying "human-in-the-loop" agents hired via gig platforms to execute AI-orchestrated crimes [19]. The task of testifying in court regarding investigation findings is unlikely to change, as the legal standard for oral testimony remains centered on human accountability and witness credibility [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, fraud examiners may shift from verifying the existence of documentation to verifying the operational legitimacy of the entities and AI agents providing that documentation.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For fraud examiners broadly, if the asymmetry in AI experimentation between criminals and institutions persists, the task of analyzing financial data to detect irregularities may become a process of constant iterative adaptation to evolving AI attack signatures [7]. Extrapolating from current synthetic identity trends, coordinating investigative efforts with law enforcement officers and attorneys could be constrained by the difficulty of attributing synthetic entities to physical actors across international borders [1]. For a subset of workers overseeing agentic commerce, the baseline for normal financial behavior may become more volatile if high-volume AI-driven transactions mask illicit flows [4][20]. The core requirement to prepare evidence for presentation in court persists unchanged because legal standards for the admissibility of evidence are governed by judicial precedent and procedural law rather than technological capacity [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the primary constraint on fraud investigation may shift from the detection of the anomaly to the attribution of the anomaly to a legal person.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For fraud examiners broadly, the persistence of autonomous agentic commerce may lead to a divergence in investigative methodologies. One outcome involves the total replacement of traditional document gathering with the analysis of immutable cryptographic proofs of identity and intent. Another rival outcome involves a return to high-touch human verification and field surveillance as symbolic AI agents become indistinguishable from humans in digital interactions. It remains unknown whether judicial systems will accept AI-generated forensic reconstructions as primary evidence without a human examiner's manual verification. The task of testifying in court regarding investigation findings likely resists full automation because the function of the witness is to provide a human guarantee of the evidence's integrity to a trier of fact [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may shift toward "cryptographic auditing," where the examiner validates the mathematical proofs of a transaction rather than the behavioral intent of the actor.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation may revert to intensified human-centric surveillance and physical verification to bypass the total erosion of digital trust.*

title: Computer Systems Analysts
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For the occupation broadly, analysts are increasingly performing AI mapping to align model capabilities with specific business requirements, a mechanism linked to higher revenue outcomes [2]. In organizations adopting agentic workflows, the task of expanding or modifying system to serve new purposes or improve work flow shifts from designing static automation to agent-first process redesign [4][10]. This shift requires the task of analyzing information processing or computation needs to move away from adding prompts to existing standard operating procedures toward the design of systemic AI workflows [12]. To address the emergence of agent sprawl, the task of coordinating and linking the computer systems within an organization now includes the deployment of orchestration tools to manage multiple autonomous agents [9]. For the occupation broadly, the task of reviewing and analyzing computer printouts and performance indicators to locate code problems is being supported by AI agents that automate the discovery and documentation of legacy mainframe logic during system migration [11]. Broadly, the task of preparing cost-benefit and return-on-investment analyses may be altered by a transition in total cost of ownership metrics toward cost-per-token as a primary performance indicator for AI infrastructure [7]. For analysts in public sector environments, the task of planning and designing computer systems must account for specific operational constraints and governance mandates to make AI operational [6]. In smart manufacturing settings, coordinating and linking computer systems involves integrating Internet of Things (IoT) data with customer relationship management platforms [1]. For a subset of workers in corporate administration, assessing the usefulness of pre-developed application packages includes the implementation of AI-powered onboarding agents [3]. In organizations utilizing cloud-based AI projects, analysts may use new attribution tools to manage inference costs [5]. For analysts specifying hardware requirements, the transition to autonomous agentic systems shifts technical bottlenecks from GPUs to CPUs and memory [8]. For analysts in the United States government, the task of coordinating and linking computer systems includes the integration of disparate state and federal identity databases, such as driver's licenses and passports, into a unified platform [13]. The task of troubleshooting program and system malfunctions is unlikely to change for physical hardware or low-level kernel failures, as these remain manual technical processes [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, analysts broadly will shift toward mapping AI capabilities to business outcomes and designing systemic workflows for autonomous agents, while subsegments in government, manufacturing, and cloud operations integrate specialized orchestration, identity integration, and cost-tracking tools.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For the occupation broadly, if current trajectories in agent-first design hold, analysts may transition from initial process mapping to the continuous optimization of dynamic systems that adapt in real time [4][10][12]. Extrapolating from current legacy migration patterns, analysts may shift from executing one-time mainframe transitions to managing permanent AI-mediated bridges that allow legacy and native systems to coexist [11]. In smart manufacturing subsegments, analysts could expand or modify systems to enable autonomous, closed-loop predictive maintenance [1]. In administrative subsegments, the focus may shift from implementing single-purpose agents to managing ecosystems of interconnected lifecycle agents [3]. For analysts in cloud-native environments, the ability to track granular inference costs could evolve from retrospective analysis to real-time resource reallocation [5][7]. The task of consulting with management to ensure agreement on system principles will persist because the governance of autonomous agent behavior requires human negotiation regarding organizational risk and accountability [8].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, analysts may shift from discrete system implementation to the continuous orchestration of adaptive agent ecosystems, with specialized roles emerging to manage the permanent technical debt of AI-legacy hybrids.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For the occupation broadly, the scope of system analysis may shift toward the auditing of emergent behaviors in fully autonomous agentic networks, though this depends on whether orchestration tools can provide transparent traceability [9][12]. A primary unknown is whether the token-cost model of total cost of ownership remains the dominant metric or is replaced by energy-based or outcome-based pricing [7]. In manufacturing and public sector subsegments, the task of planning and designing computer systems will likely resist full automation due to the high error cost associated with physical infrastructure and legal identity mandates [1][6][13]. Rival outcomes depend on whether regulatory regimes favor centralized AI orchestration or fragmented, siloed agent clusters to prevent systemic failure [6].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation evolves into a governance and auditing role, where analysts focus on the systemic stability and ethical alignment of autonomous organizational operating systems.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation fragments into highly specialized niches, where analysts manage isolated, air-gapped agent clusters mandated by strict regional or sector-specific regulatory regimes.*

title: Health Informatics Specialists
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For health informatics specialists broadly, the task of designing or implementing health information technology applications is shifting from the integration of standalone software toward the management of specialized AI infrastructure layers that enable the development of internal models [14]. The process of implementing informatics solutions is moving toward the curation of vetted digital health application libraries via centralized distribution systems, such as the CMS Medicare app library [8]. For workers in organizations deploying patient-facing chatbots, the evaluation of human-technology interactions now requires validating the clinical accuracy of these interfaces to maintain patient trust [4][5][9]. In organizations utilizing AI-driven operational platforms, the design of applications for clinical or administrative problems is increasingly focused on large-scale operational optimization [3]. For a subset of workers in organizations implementing generative AI, the task of translating nursing practice information between nurses and engineers now includes the iterative refinement of prompts to align model outputs with clinical workflows [1]. In organizations managing prior authorization, the development of decision-support mechanisms may shift toward transitioning the process from an administrative barrier to a resource model [13], as simple digitization and the implementation of FHIR APIs have proven insufficient to automate medical-necessity determinations [15]. In regions where state governments are regulating chatbots, the task of developing policies to ensure the security of patient information may be altered by new requirements for algorithmic safety audits [2]. Because AI-enabled cyberattacks increase systemic risk, the task of developing practices to ensure the confidentiality of patient information now involves integrating AI-specific threat vectors into risk assessments [7]. Regulatory calls for a crackdown on wellness AI shift the development of strategies for introducing information technology toward stricter safety and compliance criteria [11]. For a subset of workers managing mental health tools, the process of integrating technology into clinical workflows now involves developing protocols for auditing the safety of AI chatbots [16]. The task of planning, installing, repairing, or troubleshooting telehealth technology applications in homes is unlikely to change because it remains dependent on physical hardware configuration and site-specific environmental constraints [17].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, the occupation may shift toward managing centralized interoperability ecosystems and validating the clinical safety and security of AI-driven operational and patient-facing tools.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For health informatics specialists broadly, if the shift toward centralized digital health distribution persists, the task of implementing informatics solutions could evolve from custom system integration to the governance of interoperable app ecosystems [8]. Extrapolating from current regulatory trends and calls for stricter oversight, the task of developing strategies for modifying information technology may shift toward a continuous cycle of auditing algorithmic outputs to satisfy state and federal safety mandates [2][11]. If current data quality trajectories hold, the task of analyzing computer and information technologies for applicability to nursing practice may focus heavily on resolving structural data inconsistencies to enable AI scalability [10]. For a subset of workers in organizations using specialized AI infrastructure, the design of informatics solutions may shift toward the maintenance of proprietary internal imaging and diagnostic models [14]. The task of providing consultation to nurses regarding hardware or software configuration is likely to persist unchanged because the basic physical interface between the clinician and the data entry point remains a fundamental constraint of clinical environments.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupation may transition from system implementation to the governance of algorithmic compliance and the resolution of structural data barriers.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For health informatics specialists broadly, the scope of the occupation may bifurcate based on the success of global data standardization. If interoperability becomes absolute, the task of designing decision-support mechanisms could shift toward the orchestration of autonomous, cross-institutional health agents. However, if data fragmentation persists due to proprietary constraints, the occupation may return to a model of highly specialized, site-specific bespoke integration. It remains unknown whether regulatory frameworks will eventually allow for the full automation of medical-necessity determinations or if human-in-the-loop validation will remain a permanent legal requirement [15]. The core task of translating nursing practice information between clinicians and engineers resists change because the nuance of bedside clinical judgment cannot be fully captured by object-oriented models or automated translation tools.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may evolve into a role of high-level ecosystem orchestration and autonomous system governance.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation may remain centered on resolving fragmented data silos through localized, manual system translations.*

title: Information Security Analysts
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For information security analysts broadly, because non-human identities (NHIs) created by AI agents generate systemic visibility deficits [103] and critical security gaps [26], the task of regulating access to safeguard information now requires the active identification and elimination of orphaned NHIs [86][93]. Because high-capability models such as Claude Mythos [15] and GPT-5.4-Cyber [85] enable the autonomous discovery of software vulnerabilities at scale [109][125], the zero-day timeline is collapsing [30], shifting the task of performing risk assessments from periodic audits toward the use of the Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) for rapid prioritization [116]. Because AI-assisted supply chain attacks now target open-source repositories [9] and utilize self-propagating worms to steal developer tokens [128][132], the task of monitoring current reports of computer viruses must incorporate provenance auditing of third-party dependencies [2][94]. In organizations using agentic security tools, the task of responding to computer security breaches shifts from manual triage to the supervision of AI agents that perform real-time investigation, containment, and remediation of runtime incidents [141][142][150]. Because prompt injection enables remote code execution within AI-integrated environments [102][111] and agentic memory attacks can persist across sessions [64][146], the task of performing risk assessments now includes auditing LLM-invoked native functions and identifying adversarial prompt patterns [98][133][138]. Training users and promoting security awareness is unlikely to change yet because industrialized social engineering [10] and AI-boosted voice phishing [95] continue to exploit human cognitive biases and impersonate IT support via collaboration platforms [115][148].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, analysts broadly may transition toward behavioral detection and provenance auditing while integrating specialized governance for non-human identities and prompt-injection risk assessment.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For information security analysts broadly, if the collapse of the zero-day timeline [30] and the rise of agentic attack speeds [22] persist, the task of performing risk assessments may shift focus from mean time to detection toward closing the "post-alert gap" via automated remediation workflows [60][105]. In organizations using automated reasoning frameworks, the task of documenting computer security and emergency measures policies may transition from manual audit logs to using formal verification to produce mathematically proven compliance results [72][79]. For a subset of workers in organizations deploying autonomous agents, because agent intent is an insufficient security proxy [36], the task of modifying computer security files may pivot toward the real-time governance of agent permissions using specialized governance toolkits [31][37]. Extrapolating from current quantum computing warnings [82], the mechanism for encrypting data transmissions will likely shift toward the deployment of post-quantum cryptographic standards to maintain confidentiality [43]. Reviewing violations of computer security procedures and discussing them with violators persists as a human-centric task because correcting behavioral errors requires qualitative social judgment and interpersonal negotiation [10].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, analysts broadly may move toward auditing automated remediation speed and post-quantum encryption, while the core of policy enforcement in agentic environments shifts toward real-time permission governance.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For information security analysts broadly, the trajectory of agentic attack and defense speeds suggests a potential state of equilibrium where the task of erecting firewalls may transition from blocking specific traffic to managing the systemic "trust layer" between autonomous entities [69][140]. In organizations where the zero-day timeline has effectively vanished [30], the task of performing risk assessments may shift from identifying vulnerabilities to managing the trade-offs of "proactive cyber" strategies that anticipate attacker moves before they manifest [13]. A critical unknown remains whether the industrialization of AI-mediated narratives [84] will render human-led security awareness training entirely obsolete or if it will necessitate a return to air-gapped, human-verified communication protocols for critical infrastructure. The task of conferring with users to discuss data access needs is likely to resist full automation even at this horizon, as these interactions are governed by organizational politics, legal liabilities, and the need for human accountability in catastrophic failure scenarios.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may evolve into a high-level orchestration role, where analysts govern the strategic parameters and ethical constraints of competing AI security agents.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the proliferation of AI-driven systemic risk may force a fragmentation of the occupation, with a subset of analysts specializing in the maintenance of "analog" or human-only secure enclaves to ensure survival during AI-driven outages.*

title: Computer and Information Research Scientists
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For computer and information research scientists broadly, the observed failure of current AI benchmarks [6][31] shifts the task of developing performance standards toward the creation of predictive performance frameworks [15], the empirical determination of minimum rater sufficiency [9], and the adoption of symbolic logic benchmarks such as lambda calculus [61]. Because new architectures may reduce energy use by 100x [18] and enable models to become leaner during the learning process [28], the application of theoretical expertise to create or apply new technology focuses on energy-efficient scaling and long-context reasoning efficiency [62]. For a subset of researchers specializing in safety and alignment, the requirements to protect against harmful manipulation [7], evaluate behavioral dispositions [8], and implement training that enables models to signal uncertainty [48] alter how they conduct logical analyses of technical problems. For researchers focusing on systems architecture, the deployment of gigawatt-scale datacenters [4], innovations in tensor, context, and expert parallelism [12], and the native execution of PyTorch workflows on TPUs [52] change the mechanisms used in designing computers and the software that runs them. For those in embodied AI, the development of visually grounded interactive planning [10][11] and the pursuit of world models [36] change how they participate in multidisciplinary projects. In regions where legal constraints regarding "unauthorized distillation"—the use of competitor model outputs to train smaller models [60]—are enforced, the methods used to develop solutions involving computer software are constrained. In resource-strapped contexts, as reported in several developing nations [14][22], theoretical expertise shifts toward the design of frugal models that maintain utility under severe hardware limitations. Tasks involving the approval, prepare, monitor, and adjust operational budgets are unlikely to change, as these remain governed by institutional financial constraints [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, the occupation broadly pivots toward energy-efficient architectures and dynamic evaluation standards, while specialized subsegments navigate extreme-scale infrastructure, grounded robotic reasoning, and increasing legal constraints on model distillation.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For computer and information research scientists broadly, if current trajectories in decentralized training [19], on-the-job learning architectures [26], and decoupled training frameworks [50] hold, the reduction in iterative experimentation costs may shift how they analyze problems to develop solutions involving computer hardware and software. Extrapolating from research into first-principles reasoning for synthetic datasets [35] and automated domain adaptation [47], the application of theoretical expertise may move toward the design of systems capable of autonomous architectural refinement. For a subset of workers specializing in quantum computing, the establishment of logical qubit standards [17] and the application of quantum-boosted AI for predicting chaos [41][42] may stabilize the mechanisms used in designing computers. The task of consulting with users, management, vendors, and technicians to determine computing needs will persist unchanged because system requirements remain tied to human organizational objectives [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupation may shift toward the design of self-optimizing architectures and synthetic-data-driven research, reducing manual theoretical iteration while increasing focus on the foundational constraints of quantum and decentralized systems.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For computer and information research scientists broadly, the scope of the occupation may diverge based on whether compute resources remain centralized or become fully distributed. One outcome involves the transition of the role from designing specific architectures to managing recursive improvement cycles, where the application of theoretical expertise is used to audit AI-generated mathematical models [5]. A rival outcome emerges if geopolitical fragmentation and resource scarcity lead to a permanent bifurcation of the field into "frontier" researchers in high-compute hubs and "frugal" researchers in resource-constrained regions [14][22][63]. The extent to which quantum-AI integration can resolve current scaling bottlenecks remains an unresolvable uncertainty at this horizon. Even in these scenarios, the core task of conducting logical analyses of technical problems resists full automation, as the definition of "solution" continues to evolve alongside shifting human and organizational needs [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation evolves into a supervisory role overseeing autonomous research cycles and recursive architectural optimization.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation fragments into distinct geopolitical castes, with one focusing on extreme-scale frontier models and the other on ultra-frugal, localized hardware constraints.*

title: Computer User Support Specialists
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For computer user support specialists broadly, the integration of AI agents into IT service management platforms [3] and the increase in helpdesk impersonation attacks via enterprise collaboration tools [1][4][6] alter the mechanisms of user interaction. Because AI agents are increasingly utilized for initial triage and ticket intake [3], the task of answering user inquiries regarding computer software or hardware operation is partially shifted to automated systems. Simultaneously, the use of fake authentication pages [2] and the impersonation of support staff via Microsoft Teams [4][6] necessitate a transition in how specialists investigate and resolve problems, moving from trust-based interactions to rigid identity-verification protocols. The introduction of hardened security warnings for Remote Desktop connections [5] and the deployment of complex "second-chance" setup dialogs in Windows 11 [7] increase the volume of support requests centered on guiding users through onboarding and explaining security prompts. This environment increases the importance of maintaining records of daily data communication transactions and remedial actions [O*NET 8] to provide forensic audit trails during security breaches [1]. Physical tasks, such as setting up equipment for employee use [O*NET 2], are unlikely to change due to the requirement for manual cable installation and physical hardware placement.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, the occupation will shift toward a hybrid model where AI agents manage routine triage and human specialists focus on high-stakes identity verification and guiding users through security-hardened system behaviors.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For computer user support specialists broadly, if current trajectories of AI-driven helpdesk governance [3] and identity-based attacks [2][4][6] hold, the task of investigating and resolving problems may move toward a zero-trust operational model. In this scenario, the specialist's role in granting access or resetting credentials is constrained by automated cryptographic verification, reducing human discretion in identity adjudication. This shift may alter how specialists develop training materials and procedures for users [O*NET 11], prioritizing secure identity hygiene over basic software navigation. The need to confer with staff, users, and management to establish requirements for new systems [O*NET 6] persists because organizational workflows and internal political constraints remain too idiosyncratic for algorithmic standardization.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, symbolic support tasks may be largely governed by AI agents, leaving human specialists to manage the exceptions and failures of these automated systems.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For computer user support specialists broadly, the trajectory of the occupation may diverge based on the evolution of synthetic social engineering. In one outcome, symbolic support for software and account access is fully automated, leaving human specialists to focus almost exclusively on performing minor repairs to hardware [O*NET 5] and peripheral equipment. In a competing outcome, a verified human support tier may emerge for high-security environments where automated identity adjudication is viewed as a vulnerability to advanced synthetic impersonation [4][6]. It remains unknown whether AI can reliably distinguish between biological human social engineering and synthetic impersonation without producing excessive false positives. The requirement to inspect equipment and read order sheets to prepare for delivery to users [O*NET 12] resists change due to the physical variability of hardware shipments and logistics.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may split into a hardware-centric technical role focused on physical maintenance.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, human specialists may be repositioned as the primary trust anchors for identity verification in high-security environments to counter synthetic impersonation.*

title: Computer Network Architects
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For network architects broadly, the transition from centralized AI training to decentralized inferencing is altering how they develop conceptual, logical, or physical network designs to support edge-based computing [9]. For these architects, the emergence of cost per token as a primary efficiency metric modifies the way they evaluate network designs to prioritize low-latency paths that reduce total cost of ownership [5]. In regions experiencing geopolitical instability, such as Asia and the Gulf, architects are revising how they develop disaster recovery plans to mitigate the risk of physical infrastructure strikes [3][4]. For a subsegment of workers designing hyper-scale AI clusters, including sites in India, the requirement for multi-gigawatt capacities shifts the process of determining specific network hardware or software requirements toward proprietary high-bandwidth fabrics [1][2][8]. For a subset of architects in defense settings, the requirement for mission-readiness modifies how they develop and implement solutions for network problems to ensure resilient data flows under stress [6]. For a subsegment of specialists in quantum networking, the introduction of specialized switches allows them to research and test new or modified hardware or software products that bridge disparate quantum modalities [7]. Standard local area network configurations for general office use are unlikely to change because they do not face the extreme power or latency constraints of AI-specific infrastructure [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, network architects will shift toward designing decentralized inferencing fabrics and optimizing for token-cost efficiency, while subsegments focus on gigawatt-scale power constraints and quantum modality translation.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For network architects broadly, if the trend toward decentralized inferencing holds, the process of developing conceptual, logical, or physical network designs may shift toward managing massive, coordinated fleets of small, connected data centers [9]. For the subsegment of hyper-scale architects, extrapolating from the deployment of gigawatt-scale sites suggests that capacity planning and the process of adjusting network sizes to meet volume demands will be increasingly constrained by electrical grid limits and thermal dissipation [1][2][8]. In regions where geopolitical volatility persists, the process of developing disaster recovery plans may shift from simple redundancy to systemic regional decoupling to prevent single-point failures [3][4]. For the subsegment of quantum network specialists, the scaling of modality-bridging switches may enable the design of quantum intranets that extend beyond isolated nodes [7]. Standard enterprise routing protocols are likely to persist unchanged due to the immense installed base of legacy hardware and global interoperability standards [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupation may bifurcate into specialists in regionally decoupled resilience, architects of energy-constrained hyper-scale fabrics, and designers of distributed AI inferencing networks.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For network architects broadly, the structural tension between the efficiency of centralized gigawatt-scale AI factories and the resilience of decentralized edge networks remains an unresolvable uncertainty [1][9]. It remains unknown whether quantum networking will result in a fully integrated global fabric or remain a parallel, specialized infrastructure for specific compute tasks [7]. For the subsegment of hyper-scale architects, it is uncertain whether physical site size will hit a hard limit imposed by energy grid capacity or if new power distribution technologies will allow further centralization [1][2][8]. The fundamental physical constraints of signal propagation speed and the necessity of physical cabling will resist change even at this horizon.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the field converges on massive, centralized AI factories where network design is subsumed by power and thermal engineering.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, geopolitical instability and the requirements of real-time inferencing force a permanent shift toward hyper-distributed, resilient edge architectures.*

title: Telecommunications Engineering Specialists
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subset of workers in the oil and gas sector, specialists in regions managing rapid 5G consumer expansion, Chinese telecommunications organizations operating in the United States, organizations integrating commercial satellite services into defense infrastructure, and those managing legacy cellular migrations, operational focuses are diverging based on localized regulatory and industrial drivers [1][2][3][4][5]. In the oil and gas subsegment, the transition of private 5G to a business-critical utility alters the process of assessing existing facilities' needs [O*NET] by prioritizing safety-critical connectivity over basic access [1]. This shift requires a more rigorous approach to estimating costs for system implementation [O*NET] using total cost of ownership (TCO) models that incorporate workforce safety and operational reliability [1]. In regions experiencing massive consumer scale-up, the need to review and evaluate requests for system modifications [O*NET] increases to manage network capacity as user bases scale [2]. For Chinese telecommunications organizations facing regulatory crackdowns in the US, the role shifts toward implementing system renovation projects [O*NET] specifically for the purpose of migrating or decommissioning data center infrastructure [3]. In organizations integrating commercial satellite services into defense infrastructure, specialists must consult with users, administrators, and engineers to identify technical requirements [O*NET] for incorporating off-the-shelf commercial components into military budgets and systems [5]. For a subsegment managing legacy-to-5G transitions, implementing system renovation projects [O*NET] may increasingly rely on specialized migration frameworks to accelerate the phase-out of legacy cellular protocols [4]. Inspecting sites to determine physical configuration [O*NET] remains unlikely to change because physical conduit pathways and tower placements are constrained by existing urban and industrial footprints.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, specialists in these specific subsegments and regions will treat 5G and satellite infrastructure as either a safety-critical utility, a massive-scale consumer requirement, a regulatory liability, a military integration target, or a legacy migration objective.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For these same subsegments and organizations, if current trajectories hold, the increased reliance on 5G for safety and mass-scale connectivity may lead to more stringent requirements for developing telecommunications disaster recovery plans [O*NET] [1][2]. Because the network serves as a strategic backbone in industrial settings, the implementation of backup or recovery procedures [O*NET] may evolve to support near-zero latency for safety-critical data [1]. In high-growth consumer regions, the requirement to monitor and analyze system performance [O*NET] may shift toward the management of automated traffic steering to handle billion-user loads [2]. For organizations undergoing regulatory-driven exits, the focus may shift to documenting procedures for hardware and software installation and use [O*NET] as part of permanent asset handover or site closures [3]. For those managing cellular migrations, the task of testing and evaluating hardware and software [O*NET] will likely shift from compatibility testing to the validation of fully decommissioned legacy environments [4]. In defense contexts, testing and evaluating hardware and software [O*NET] may focus on the interoperability between proprietary military standards and rapidly evolving commercial satellite protocols [5]. However, the need to consult with users, administrators, and engineers to identify technical requirements [O*NET] will persist, as business and safety protocols remain grounded in human-defined operational constraints.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the role for these subsets will shift toward ensuring the disaster resilience and automated performance of high-density networks, the structured decommissioning of regulated assets, or the interoperability of commercial and defense satellite systems.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For specialists in these settings, the long-term trajectory depends on whether global telecommunications standards converge or fragment further along geopolitical and security lines. In organizations integrating commercial satellite and 5G services, the task of implementing controls to provide security for operating systems, software, and data [O*NET] may be dictated by competing national security mandates, creating divergent technical silos [3][5]. The extent to which automated system performance analysis [O*NET] can replace human-led capacity planning remains an unresolvable uncertainty. Despite these shifts, the requirement to document technical specifications and operating standards [O*NET] will resist change, as the high error cost of telecommunications failure necessitates permanent, human-readable records of system architecture.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, specialists in these contexts operate within a highly commercialized ecosystem where the distinction between private, public, and defense infrastructure is blurred by the ubiquity of commercial off-the-shelf satellite and 5G services.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, specialists operate within fragmented "technology stacks" where regulatory exits and security mandates force the maintenance of entirely separate, non-interoperable hardware and software environments for different geopolitical regions.*

title: Database Administrators
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For database administrators broadly, the introduction of autonomous agents and natural language interfaces may alter core operational and security workflows. AI-driven storage optimization tools could reduce the manual effort required to identify, evaluate and recommend hardware or software technologies to achieve desired database performance by automating capacity forecasting [1]. The deployment of large language models for text-to-SQL interfaces may shift the task to write and code logical and physical database descriptions toward the auditing of AI-generated queries [2]. For a subset of workers managing third-party SaaS integrations, the emergence of data access benchmarks is introducing new criteria for evaluating vendor egress fees and access constraints [3]. For a subset of workers in high-intelligence data environments, the task to test programs or databases and correct errors is increasingly focused on maintaining data integrity as a prerequisite for AI reliability [4]. The task to plan, coordinate, and implement security measures to safeguard information is being reinforced by the risk of "data extinction events" caused by autonomous AI agents executing destructive queries on production databases [5][6]. The task to train users and answer questions is unlikely to change in the near term due to the persistent requirement for human-led knowledge transfer within organizational hierarchies.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, database administrators may transition from manual capacity planning and query coding to the oversight of predictive tools, while security tasks intensify to mitigate risks posed by autonomous AI agents.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For database administrators broadly, if current trajectories in automated provisioning and natural language interfaces hold, the task to select and enter codes to monitor database performance may move toward a high-level auditing role [1][2]. Practitioners could spend less time on routine hardware recommendations and more time validating the efficiency of AI-generated query plans to prevent performance degradation [2]. The necessity to test programs or databases and correct errors persists, as recovering from complex data corruption or structural logical conflicts often requires human architectural context that automated tools cannot currently replicate [5][6].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the role may evolve from active manual provisioning and coding to the auditing and performance-tuning of automated database management systems.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For database administrators broadly, the long-term trajectory suggests two rival outcomes. In one scenario, the complete abstraction of storage and query layers via AI could render the task of recommending hardware technologies obsolete, shifting the occupation toward the development of standards and guidelines for the use and acquisition of software [1][2]. In a competing scenario, the increasing complexity of hyper-scale, distributed environments may maintain a need for specialists who manually override AI to manage extreme performance edge-cases [1]. It remains unknown whether future database management systems will fully decouple logical data modeling from physical resource allocation. The requirement to train users and answer questions is likely to resist change, as this remains tied to human organizational communication needs [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may transition into a governance-focused role as routine performance and query tasks become fully automated.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation may bifurcate, with a specialized class of engineers managing physical and logical constraints that AI cannot optimize.*

title: Database Architects
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For database architects broadly, and for a subset of workers in AI-integrated, industrial, or healthcare settings, current architectural shifts are driven by the need to remove obstacles to AI adoption. For the broad occupation, the task of developing database architectural strategies is shifting as enterprises replace traditional relational structures with "AI-ready" stacks that prioritize unstructured data handling and vector databases [7]. The requirement to create and enforce database development standards may be updated to address the liabilities associated with unrecoverable or poorly governed data used in AI training [6]. Within the AI-integrated subsegment, architects may alter how they develop data models for applications by integrating vector stores and graph-based schemas to provide persistent, company-wide memory and hybrid Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) capabilities [1][5]. In industrial settings, the task of developing methods for integrating different products is focusing on unifying fragmented operational data to enable real-time intelligence [3]. In healthcare contexts, a shift toward new health IT categories is altering how architectural strategies are developed to support systemic data needs [4]. Additionally, the task of designing databases to support business applications may shift toward implementing granular access controls specifically for autonomous AI agents [2]. However, the task of developing data models for primary systems of record, such as core financial ledgers, is unlikely to change due to the catastrophic error cost associated with probabilistic storage in these environments [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, database architects will shift toward designing "AI-ready" stacks and hybrid vector-relational models, while the broader occupation will integrate data liability constraints into development standards.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For the subset of architects managing AI-ready stacks and agentic data environments, if the trajectory toward "AI-ready" infrastructure holds, the task of writing and coding logical and physical database descriptions may be partially automated. This automation would likely involve tools that map natural language business requirements directly to vector-relational schema elements [2][7]. Extrapolating from hybrid RAG deployments, the task of refining system performance and functionality may shift toward managing semantic synchronization to prevent drift between embedding models and source data [1]. This shift could reduce the manual effort required for documenting database schemas, as orchestration layers manage the relationship between raw data and its semantic representation [2]. Despite these shifts, the task of identifying and evaluating industry trends to advise upper management will persist, as the selection of infrastructure involves strategic trade-offs and cost constraints that remain human-led [4].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, database design for this subsegment may shift toward automated schema mapping and the management of semantic synchronization, reducing the burden of manual documentation.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For the subset of architects in AI-integrated and industrial environments, the long-term trajectory suggests a tension between autonomous optimization and regulatory auditability. If AI agents successfully automate the task of developing database architectural strategies based on real-time usage patterns, the human role in defining static physical descriptions may diminish [3]. A rival outcome exists where stringent data provenance laws make the task of documenting and communicating database schemas more rigorous to ensure the auditability of AI-generated outputs [6]. It remains unknown whether the relational model will persist as a primary architectural primitive or be subsumed by more fluid, non-schema-dependent structures [7]. The task of establishing and calculating optimum values for database parameters is likely to resist full automation in high-stakes environments where failure costs remain catastrophic [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the role may shift toward high-level oversight of autonomous architectural agents that dynamically optimize data structures in real-time.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the role may shift toward a regulatory and forensic function, focusing on the strict documentation and provenance of data stacks to meet legal audit requirements.*

title: Data Warehousing Specialists
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For data warehousing specialists broadly, the transition toward integrated data fabrics to support AI business value may alter the development of data warehouse process models [4] and the design of warehouse database structures [7]. AI-driven tools for storage optimization may reduce manual over-provisioning by predicting usage patterns [1], which could change how specialists balance optimization of data access with resource utilization factors [8]. For a subset of workers in industrial settings, the requirement for data integrity to support industrial intelligence may increase the rigor applied when verifying the structure, accuracy, or quality of warehouse data [6]. For a subset of workers in organizations deploying AI agents, the need to resolve data access bottlenecks may alter the implementation of metadata processes and frameworks to ensure data is governable for autonomous consumption [3]. In organizations integrating data from specific enterprise SaaS vendors, poor data access and egress constraints may increase the complexity of developing and implementing data extraction procedures [5]. Mapping data between source systems, data warehouses, and data marts [8] is unlikely to change in this period because it requires deep semantic understanding of legacy business logic that current predictive tools do not address.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, data warehousing specialists may shift toward implementing data fabrics and AI-driven storage optimization, while a subset may specialize in optimizing metadata for AI agents and integrity verification in industrial settings.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For data warehousing specialists broadly, if trajectories in data fabric adoption [4] and predictive storage [1] hold, resource management may shift from manual tuning toward the governance of autonomous scaling policies. Specialists could spend less time on the technical configuration of storage volumes and more on defining operational constraints for AI-managed volumes. For those supporting AI agents, the role may shift toward the continuous governance of agent-ready data pipelines to maintain the precision required for autonomous consumption [3]. In industrial contexts, the task of implementing business rules via stored procedures or middleware [8] may be increasingly driven by the requirements of real-time visibility foundations [2]. The task of verifying the structure, accuracy, or quality of warehouse data [8] is likely to persist as a core human responsibility due to the high error costs associated with corporate financial and regulatory reporting.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupation may transition from manual resource tuning toward the governance of automated storage orchestration and the maintenance of specialized data environments optimized for AI agents.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For data warehousing specialists broadly, the long-term trajectory suggests two rival outcomes regarding the nature of the warehouse. In one scenario, the convergence of predictive resource management [1], industrial unification [2], and agent-centric access [3] could lead to the emergence of "liquid" data architectures where static database structures are replaced by AI-managed ephemeral environments. In a competing scenario, strict regulatory requirements for data provenance and auditability could freeze the reliance on manually defined, transparent warehouse structures to ensure legal compliance. It remains unknown whether future compute-storage separation technologies will render the concept of "warehousing" as a distinct architectural pattern obsolete. The necessity of maintaining standards, such as organization or nomenclature, for the design of data warehouse elements [8] may resist change due to the fundamental need for human-readable organizational schemas.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may evolve into the governance of ephemeral, AI-managed data environments that assemble and disassemble based on real-time agent requirements.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation may consolidate around the maintenance of rigid, transparently mapped structures mandated by global data auditability and provenance laws.*
