title: Network and Computer Systems Administrators
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For network and computer systems administrators broadly, the integration of AI-driven IT operations tools shifts the task to maintain and administer computer networks from manual configuration toward the oversight of automated remediation systems [10][24]. Because AI-driven analytics identify specific patterns of over-provisioning, the task to analyze network and server resource consumption may shift toward the systematic reduction of redundant data storage to lower operational costs [5]. For administrators managing autonomous agents, the task to perform data backups and disaster recovery operations now includes implementing state-rollbacks to mitigate erroneous actions taken by rogue agents [9]. In organizations deploying updated enterprise browser fleets, the task to install and upgrade software expands to include the orchestration of AI-generated summaries and integrated browser-based workflows [17]. For administrators securing legacy environments, the task to replace defective components now involves the aggressive decommissioning of discontinued hardware that cannot be patched against persistent botnet threats [13][16]. For a subset of administrators managing Cisco firewall hardware, the task to diagnose, troubleshoot, and resolve network and system problems may require executing physical cold start procedures to clear persistent backdoors [27]. In environments using Linux-based networking, the task to maintain and administer computer networks involves replacing legacy hardware as AI-driven bug reports lead to the removal of old network drivers from the kernel [21]. For administrators managing identity and access, the task to plan, coordinate, and implement network security measures includes auditing privileged AI agent roles to prevent identity takeover attacks [25][28]. Physical cabling and the manual installation of rack-mounted hardware are unlikely to change yet because these tasks require precise physical manipulation in diverse site environments.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, the occupation shifts from direct system configuration to the management of autonomous agents and the aggressive decommissioning of legacy hardware that cannot support modern security or AI-driven management.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For a subset of workers in large-scale data center environments, if current trajectories hold, the task to design, configure, and test computer hardware shifts from managing monolithic facilities toward orchestrating a distributed network of smaller, connected nodes to support AI inferencing [26]. Extrapolating from current GPU power trends, the task to monitor network performance may require specialized expertise in tracking GPU efficiency and estimating total AI power consumption to manage high operational costs [18][22]. For administrators in cloud-native settings, the task to plan, coordinate, and implement network security measures could shift toward the management of frontier agents that autonomously conduct security testing and cloud operations [2]. Fundamental network protocols and the basic logic of subnetting and routing are likely to persist unchanged because these standards provide the essential interoperability required across heterogeneous hardware vendors.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, for those in AI-intensive settings, the occupation evolves into a specialized role focused on the energy efficiency and distributed orchestration of high-compute infrastructure.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For a subset of workers in AI-intensive settings, the scope of the occupation may bifurcate based on the resolution of energy constraints and hardware autonomy. One outcome involves the transition of the administrator into a site-reliability role focused on the physical maintenance of hyper-dense, decentralized compute nodes. A competing outcome involves the near-total abstraction of the network layer, where the administrator focuses exclusively on the policy-level governance of autonomous agent fleets. It remains unknown whether energy scarcity will force a return to highly centralized, manually optimized hubs. The necessity for physical intervention during catastrophic hardware failure resists change even at this horizon.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation evolves into a physical infrastructure specialist managing the hardware substrate for decentralized AI.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation shifts entirely toward high-level policy governance and auditing of autonomous network agents.*

title: Computer Programmers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For this occupation broadly, the deployment of agentic coding tools and high-capacity models like GPT-5.5 shifts the task of writing, analyzing, review, and rewriting programs from manual authorship toward the supervision and orchestration of agentic outputs [14][15][17][19][20][21][24][25][26]. The mechanism for correcting errors is modified by the introduction of cross-model review features and updated debugging capabilities, which provide automated second opinions to verify logical consistency [5][22]. For a subset of workers in the logistics subsegment, specialized AI agents automate the task of writing, update, and maintain computer programs to handle specific jobs such as rate complexity [2]. In organizations using high-exposure AI tools, the demand for junior developers whose core tasks center on routine authorship may decline as employers shift toward workers capable of managing AI systems [3][27]. For tech workers in East Asian markets, as reported in China, the creation of "AI doubles" introduces a new layer of personal automation for routine programming tasks [10]. In the Android development subsegment, the introduction of tools designed for robotic consumption rather than human readability shifts the task of writing programs toward machine-to-machine communication [11]. The task of conducting trial runs of programs is complicated by "vibe coding," where high-level prompting without rigorous verification may introduce silent logical failures that evade superficial testing [8]. The task of consulting with managerial, engineering, and technical personnel to clarify program intent is unlikely to change, as agentic systems still require precise human specifications to prevent logical drift [5].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, computer programmers may transition from manual code authorship to the supervision of agentic generation, while the demand for entry-level roles focused on routine authorship may decline.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For this occupation broadly, if the availability of open-source agentic tools offsets the costs of proprietary systems [1], the task of performing or directing revision, repair, or expansion of existing programs may shift toward iterative, self-correcting agent loops [5]. Extrapolating from the integration of AI-driven development platforms for enterprises [6][12] and the deployment of agentic "co-workers" in cloud environments [14][25], the manual effort required to write, update, and maintain computer programs for specific operational tasks may decrease. The task of compiling and writing documentation of program development is likely to persist as a human-led activity to ensure system auditability and regulatory compliance in high-stakes environments [2]. The task of investigating whether networks, workstations, or peripheral equipment are responding to program instructions is unlikely to change, as symbolic agents lack the physical observability required for hardware-level troubleshooting [12].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupation may shift toward the validation and orchestration of AI-generated logic, with routine maintenance becoming increasingly automated across enterprise settings.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For this occupation broadly, the long-term trajectory depends on whether AI-generated code remains legible to human programmers. One plausible outcome is that the task of preparing detailed workflow charts and diagrams is replaced by the management of autonomous agents that handle the end-to-end lifecycle of maintaining computer programs [4][12][17]. A competing outcome is that the accumulation of opaque, AI-generated legacy code creates a complexity trap, where the loss of human mental models forces a return to manual revision and repair of critical systems. It remains unknown whether a standardized orchestration layer can prevent the total decoupling of program intent from executable code [26]. The requirement for human accountability in the final approval of code for safety-critical systems resists change even at this horizon.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may evolve into a high-level architectural role where humans define system goals and agents execute the entire programming lifecycle.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the accumulation of unreadable AI-generated code may necessitate a resurgence of manual programming to recover and stabilize critical infrastructure.*

title: Software Developers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For software developers broadly, the task of modify existing software is shifting from manual authorship toward the auditing and integration of AI-generated code, as some large technology firms report that up to 75% of their code is now AI-generated [79] and newer models can independently debug and operate software [83]. The task of develop or direct software system testing or validation procedures is incorporating cross-model reviews to provide automated second opinions [17] and the deployment of specialized models to identify and patch vulnerabilities in legacy codebases [58][60][62][74][77]. Because AI-driven vulnerability discovery now outpaces human remediation capacity, the volume of patching tasks is increasing [25][78][97]. For open-source maintainers tasked to supervise the work of programmers, the vetting burden is increasing because industrialized social engineering and self-propagating supply chain worms are targeting package registries [6][16][21][71][72][88]. For a subset of entry-level developers in regions where engineering curricula are pivoting, the task of modify existing software is being automated to the extent that traditional implementation roles are contracting [4][104]. For a subset of workers in XR and game development, the task of design, develop and modify software systems is moving toward "vibe coding" using modular blocks [2] or single-prompt generation [49], though this may increase the prevalence of unstable code and production errors [13][39][103]. In high-performance computing contexts, the task of modify existing software now includes using system-wide visibility toolkits to identify and optimize agent-driven code inefficiencies [111]. The task of analyze user needs and software requirements is unlikely to change significantly because agentic tools cannot independently reconcile design feasibility with volatile real-world time and cost constraints [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, routine implementation tasks shift toward agentic automation, while the developer's role pivots toward the security vetting, remediation, and integration of AI-generated contributions.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For software developers broadly, if current trajectories in agent orchestration hold, the task of design, develop and modify software systems may shift from writing discrete code to managing registries of specialized AI agents that execute complex workflows [29][32][37][59][101]. This transition may introduce a new requirement to manage "daemons" specifically designed to clean up the operational residues and errors produced by autonomous agents [56]. For a subset of developers implementing AI retrieval systems, the task of store, retrieve, and manipulate data for analysis may shift from building static pipelines to implementing dynamic memory management with biological decay logic to reduce context window noise [94]. For those in security-critical subsegments, the task of develop or direct software system testing or validation procedures could integrate LLM-driven mutation testing to automate compliance checks [3] and the use of SDKs for agent governance and audit trails [26]. The task of determine system performance standards is unlikely to change because it remains anchored to physical hardware limitations, such as GPU communication bottlenecks and tensor parallelism constraints [8][20].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the developer's role shifts toward the orchestration and governance of autonomous agent swarms, with a new focus on the operational cleanup of agent-generated residues.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For software developers broadly, the scope of the occupation may diverge based on the resolution of the tension between AI-generated scale and systemic stability. In one scenario, the task of design, develop and modify software systems transitions into a purely architectural role where humans define high-level constraints and objective functions, while the actual implementation is entirely handled by an interconnected agentic fabric. In a rival scenario, the accumulation of "AI slop" and the proliferation of legacy agent-generated errors could force a return to manual, high-assurance authorship for core infrastructure to prevent systemic collapse. It remains unknown whether human oversight can effectively scale to the volume of code produced by multi-agent systems. The task of confer with systems analysts and engineers to obtain information on project limitations is likely to persist even at this horizon, as the definition of "limitations" will continue to depend on human organizational priorities and physical resource scarcity.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation evolves into a high-level system architecture role, focusing on the definition of constraints rather than the implementation of logic.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, a crisis of systemic instability leads to a resurgence in manual, high-assurance programming for critical infrastructure to purge accumulated agentic errors.*

title: Software Quality Assurance Analysts and Testers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For software quality assurance analysts and testers broadly, the deployment of LLM-based bug-hunting tools such as Claude Mythos [16][18] and Project Glasswing [9], alongside open-source models with similar discovery capabilities [22], shifts the task of identifying, analyzing, and documenting problems with program function toward the triage and validation of AI-generated reports. The proliferation of low-quality AI-generated code—described as "AI slop"—increases the manual burden of identifying program deviance from standards, as testers must distinguish functional defects from synthetic noise [3]. AI agents capable of debugging code and operating software [21] may reduce the time required for performing initial debugging procedures by reviewing configuration files and logs. In organizations adopting automated reasoning and LLM-based mutation testing [1][12], the task of developing testing programs may shift toward managing formal verification checks and compliance parameters. For a subset of workers in the autonomous vehicle subsegment, operational failures in urban environments [2][8] and the redefinition of acceptable performance thresholds for lane-keeping [23] necessitate more rigorous edge-case validation when designing test plans and scenarios. The task of investigating customer problems referred by technical support is unlikely to change in this horizon because it requires interpreting unstructured, environment-specific user reports that lack standardized logs.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, the occupation may diverge between a high-volume verification role focused on filtering AI-generated code and a specialized validation role focused on non-deterministic AI outputs.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For testers in high-complexity and safety-critical settings, if current trajectories hold, the task of monitoring program performance may shift from detecting explicit crashes toward identifying "quiet" failures and subtle performance drift [7]. Extrapolating from the development of realism-gap measurements in user simulators [10], the task of identifying problems with content for AI-driven applications may transition toward the orchestration of synthetic user populations to stress-test edge cases. The use of AI to predict performance across tasks [11] could shift the task of planning test schedules toward a dynamic, risk-based model where testing resources are allocated to the most unstable system modules. Because the complexity of agentic AI tool testing increases, the task of configuring recreations of software production environments may shift toward the use of scalable tool simulators [15]. Participating in product design reviews to provide input on functional requirements will likely persist unchanged because it depends on human negotiation of schedules and organizational priorities.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the analyst's role in high-complexity environments may transition toward the orchestration of automated validation frameworks rather than the execution of discrete test cases.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For the occupation broadly, and particularly in high-complexity settings, the scope of work may shift toward high-level system auditing, where the primary task is the verification of the AI agents that manage the testing lifecycle [15][21]. A primary uncertainty remains whether automated reasoning can identify "unknown unknowns" in system architecture or if discovery remains bounded by the statistical patterns of training data. The task of developing or specifying standards to determine product quality or release readiness may resist complete automation due to the legal liability and regulatory accountability inherent in final release sign-off.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may consolidate into a high-level architectural auditing role, focusing on the systemic integrity of AI-generated and AI-tested software.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation may fragment into hyper-specialized roles focused exclusively on the verification of non-deterministic behaviors in safety-critical autonomous systems.*

title: Web Developers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For web developers broadly, the adoption of autonomous coding agents and large-scale model deployment may alter the task of writing supporting code by shifting labor from manual drafting to the orchestration of prompt-based generation [1][13][14][15][18][19]. Because some organizations report that up to 75% of their code is now AI-generated, the task of evaluating code to ensure it is properly structured shifts toward auditing outputs using cross-model review features to reduce hallucination errors [5][18]. For a subset of workers managing content-heavy sites, the deployment of AI-powered CMS platforms may shift the task of designing, building, or maintaining web sites toward managing automated structural deployments [3]. The task of incorporating technical considerations into web site design plans now requires optimizing site architecture so that browser-integrated AI agents can accurately parse and retrieve data for AI-led search [4][12]. For developers building modern frontend applications, writing supporting code may include integrating live AI browser agents and browser-native prompt APIs directly into frameworks like React [6][21]. The task of monitoring security system performance logs now involves detecting supply-chain worms and malicious developer tools targeting environments via the npm registry [16][17]. While generation speeds increase, the task of evaluating code to ensure it meets industry standards must explicitly include manual verification of accessibility requirements that automated tools often neglect [7]. Analyzing user needs to determine technical requirements is unlikely to change yet because this task requires the interpersonal negotiation of ambiguous business goals and stakeholder constraints [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, web developers may transition from manual code authors to auditors of agent-generated code, while expanding their scope to include AI-agent optimization and the remediation of agent-induced technical debt.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For web developers broadly, if the availability of low-cost or open-source autonomous agents scales to offset the costs of proprietary subscriptions [1], the task of selecting programming languages, design tools, or applications may shift toward agent-led optimization based on real-time performance constraints. Extrapolating from current cross-model review capabilities, the manual effort required to perform web site tests could decrease as agents autonomously cycle through planning, implementation, and verification [5]. For workers in the CMS subsegment, the continued adoption of AI-native platforms may further reduce the necessity for manual evaluation or recommendation of server hardware or software by abstracting infrastructure management [3]. The requirement to confer with management or development teams to prioritize needs persists because these tasks involve organizational politics and subjective value judgments that resist algorithmic resolution [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupation may transition toward the orchestration of autonomous agent pipelines for code generation and verification, provided the cost of deployment remains low.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For web developers broadly, the far-term trajectory depends on whether the structural model of web applications remains dependent on manually audited codebases. One possible outcome is that the task of writing supporting code is fully abstracted, shifting the role entirely toward the design of high-level system interaction diagrams and data models [27][21]. A rival outcome is that the proliferation of agent-generated technical debt and security vulnerabilities [10][16] mandates a return to strict, human-centric manual code auditing as the primary value proposition of the occupation. It remains unknown whether browser-native AI will eventually eliminate the need for distinct web application interfaces entirely. The fundamental requirement to ensure web accessibility and privacy remains a point of resistance to full automation due to the legal and ethical necessity of human accountability [7][29].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may evolve into a system architecture role focused on defining constraints for autonomous agent ecosystems that handle all implementation and maintenance.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation may pivot toward a specialized "code forensic" role focused on the security auditing and stabilization of legacy AI-generated systems.*

title: Web and Digital Interface Designers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For the occupation broadly, the increased velocity of AI-driven site production may elevate the risk of accessibility regressions, necessitating a greater emphasis on the manual validation of test routines and schedules [4] to ensure compliance with accessibility standards [14][19]. The emergence of AI-led digital storefronts may shift the task of designing, building, or maintaining Web sites [8] from the creation of static layouts toward the orchestration of generative interfaces [11]. Concurrently, the rise of AI agents as primary intermediaries may reduce the utility of developing Web site maps and page templates [13] designed specifically for direct human browsing [2]. For designers in the media and publishing subsegment, the transition toward "zero-click" environments may pivot the development of e-commerce strategies [1] and site maps [13] away from page-view optimization toward propensity-based interaction hubs [7]. For a subset of workers in the financial services subsegment, the shift toward conversational AI may pivot the design of user interfaces [8] and user experience research [25] toward the engineering of dialogue flows [10]. In regions where regulatory mandates for AI content labeling are implemented, such as India, designers may need to incorporate technical considerations [19] to maintain continuous watermarks without impeding usability [8]. It is unlikely that the requirement to conduct user research to determine design requirements [4] will diminish, as understanding human intent remains necessary even when interactions are agent-mediated [2][7].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, the occupation broadly may shift toward accessibility auditing and agent-readable architectures, while subsegments in media and finance experience a pivot toward propensity-based hubs and conversational interfaces.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For the occupation broadly, if current trajectories toward agent-mediated commerce hold, the task of designing and maintaining Web sites [8] may pivot from visual layout creation toward the engineering of structured data environments optimized for autonomous agent navigation [2]. This shift would prioritize machine-readability over aesthetic conversion funnels for standard transactional tasks. For a subset of designers utilizing agentic design platforms, the process of developing new visual design concepts [10] may shift toward the orchestration of conversation-based iterations and editable designs rather than manual pixel manipulation [5]. However, the development and documentation of style guidelines for Web site content [9] will likely persist for high-value brand interactions where direct human sensory experience remains a primary competitive differentiator.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, interface design for a broad segment of e-commerce may shift toward agent-centric architectures, reducing the relative importance of visual layout optimization for transactional tasks.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For the occupation broadly, the far-term state depends on whether users fully delegate digital interactions to agents or whether a preference for immersive, visual browsing persists [2]. One plausible outcome involves the transition of the designer's role into an architect of non-visual interaction protocols for autonomous agents, where the "interface" consists of machine-readable constraints. A rival outcome suggests that advanced spatial prototyping tools [1] could drive a resurgence in highly complex, immersive human interfaces as a premium alternative to agent-driven automation. A critical unknown remains the rate of hardware adoption for immersive interfaces relative to the speed of agent-based automation. Even at this horizon, the necessity of incorporating technical considerations [19] regarding security, privacy, and legal compliance will resist automation due to the shifting nature of regulatory regimes.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may evolve into the design of non-visual interaction protocols for autonomous agents.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation may shift toward the design of high-fidelity immersive spatial interfaces for direct human interaction.*

title: Video Game Designers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subset of creators using agentic platforms, designers in small studios seeking publishers, and the broader occupation adopting volumetric AI: creators in prompt-based environments may automate the task of creating core game features, including storylines and role-play mechanics, by using agentic AI to generate initial implementations [4][5]. For the broader occupation, the adoption of photo-to-volume technology may reduce the manual labor required to prepare three-dimensional mock-ups [2]. In the subsegment of small studios, the use of specialized matchmaking platforms may alter how designers present new game design concepts to publishers to overcome discovery fatigue [3]. In specific organizational contexts, designers may utilize the creation of game text and dialogue within downloadable content to address corporate or legal disputes [1]. For designers focusing on sensory immersion, the integration of haptic feedback and 3D audio may shift how they devise missions, challenges, or puzzles to incorporate tactile interaction as a core mechanic [6]. The task of balancing and adjusting gameplay experiences is unlikely to change yet, as it depends on subjective human "feel" and iterative playtesting that current generative tools cannot replicate [7].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, agentic tools may automate core feature drafting for a subset of creators, while the broader occupation utilizes AI to accelerate 3D prototyping.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For the same subsets of designers and organizational contexts: if current trajectories hold and agentic tools for prompt-to-game implementation become standardized, the task of devising missions, challenges, or puzzles may shift from manual construction to the iterative refinement of AI-generated outputs [4][5]. Extrapolating from the integration of volumetric AI, designers may further reduce the time spent on preparing two-dimensional concept layouts in favor of high-fidelity, AI-driven 3D prototyping [2]. If high-fidelity haptic integration becomes a widespread industry standard, the task of preparing two-dimensional concept layouts may be superseded by immersive, sensory-driven prototypes [6]. The practice of using narrative DLC for corporate litigation is likely to remain a niche occurrence, limited by the commercial risk of incorporating legal disputes into consumer products [1]. Conducting regular design reviews likely persists unchanged because the evaluation of emotional resonance and player engagement requires human qualitative judgment [7].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, a subset of designers may transition from drafting to curating AI-generated missions and mechanics, while 3D prototyping largely replaces 2D conceptualization.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For the same subsets of designers: rival outcomes exist regarding the automation of creative logic, depending on whether agentic tools can eventually devise missions, challenges, or puzzles that maintain long-term psychological engagement [4]. It remains unknown if the capacity to turn photos into volumes will evolve to automate the creation of character biographies and role-play mechanics, or if these tasks remain human-driven to ensure narrative coherence [2][5]. One uncertainty is whether matchmaking platforms will evolve into fully automated curation systems that eliminate the need for designers to present concepts to human publishers [3]. The task of balancing gameplay to ensure commercial success resists change even at this horizon because it relies on the volatile and unpredictable nature of human player psychology [7].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, a subset of game design is reduced to the high-level orchestration and prompt-engineering of agentic systems for specific platform-based creators.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the prevalence of AI-generated content leads to a market premium on "human-authored" mechanics, preserving the manual creation of core game features to ensure commercial distinctiveness.*

title: Web Administrators
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subset of web administrators working in digital publishing, small-to-medium businesses (SMBs), and large institutional settings, technical priorities are shifting toward defensive hardening and content hygiene. In organizations adopting AI-integrated CMS platforms, the automation of serverless scaling and managed environments may reduce the manual effort required to implement updates, upgrades, and patches [1]. For administrators in publishing environments, the emergence of third-party AI scrapers [2] increases the requirement to deploy aggressive web site security measures [8] and use monitoring tools to detect unauthorized extraction patterns [1]. In large-scale institutional settings with aging content repositories, the task of reviewing web page content [16] and implementing procedures for ongoing revision [25] is becoming a primary defense against AI search engines surfacing outdated data as current facts [3]. For those in SMB environments, the adoption of automated certificate lifecycle management tools may reduce the manual overhead of implementing security measures [8] related to TLS deployment and renewal [4]. Despite these shifts, collaborating with development teams to resolve usability issues [9] is unlikely to change because user experience remains a qualitative human judgment.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, administrators in these subsegments will see a reduction in routine server and certificate maintenance offset by an increased requirement to manage index purity and deploy technical countermeasures against AI-driven scraping.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For these same subsegments of administrators, if current trajectories hold, the role may shift from operational execution to environment and access governance. Extrapolating from the move toward AI-powered, abstracted CMS tools, the task of installing or configuring web server software [17] may become a negligible part of the workflow [1]. As the market for AI content licensing matures [2], the task of implementing security measures [8] may shift from simple blocking to managing granular, identity-based levels of access and security [5]. The responsibility for ongoing web site revision [25] may evolve into a permanent "index hygiene" function, where administrators manage the lifecycle of content specifically to control how it is ingested by external AI models [3]. The core need to document application and web site changes [12] persists because audit trails remain a requirement for institutional accountability.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the technical administration of these environments will shift toward the governance of AI-managed configurations and the enforcement of content-access and ingestion protocols.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For administrators in these specific subsets, the long-term trajectory depends on the resolution of the conflict between content publishers and AI aggregators. One outcome involves the adoption of standardized, automated licensing protocols that eliminate the need for manual blocking, shifting the role toward a purely policy-driven compliance function. A rival outcome is that adversarial AI scrapers evolve to create opaque, systemic server failures, increasing the demand for deep forensic skills to determine sources of web page or server problems [6]. It remains unknown whether decentralized web protocols will replace the centralized CMS model entirely. However, the necessity to test backup or recovery plans regularly [14] will likely resist automation due to the catastrophic cost of total data loss.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the role for this subsegment may evolve into a compliance-focused function as content access and server environments become fully abstracted and automated.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the role may shift toward high-complexity forensic troubleshooting to resolve systemic failures caused by sophisticated, autonomous AI actors.*

title: Geographic Information Systems Technologists and Technicians
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For GIS technologists in regions with national 3D city-modeling initiatives, and for those involved in the design of public-sector mapping tools broadly, workflows are shifting toward the integration of open-access datasets and the revision of tool evaluation criteria. In contexts adopting open-access digital twins, the reliance on manual digitizing of maps or keyboard entry of tabular data [2] decreases as workers instead collect, compile, or integrate GIS data [2] by importing pre-existing high-fidelity 3D models [1]. Simultaneously, discourse among researchers regarding the shutdown of environmental justice mapping tools indicates a need to update the criteria used when designing graphic representations of GIS data [2] to better capture socio-environmental variables [3]. Because the latter is currently a subject of research and debate, this affect is limited to experimental workflow adjustments and the formulation of new requirements [3]. Providing technical expertise in GIS technology to clients [2] is unlikely to change in this period, as the variability of organizational needs still requires human-mediated technical support.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, for technologists in open-data regions and those designing public-sector tools, the role shifts from primary data creation toward the integration of standardized 3D models and the refinement of spatial analysis criteria.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For technologists in urban-modeling regions and those developing specialized spatial tools, the focus of maintaining or modifying existing GIS databases [2] may shift toward synchronization and version control if current trajectories in open-access digital twins persist [1]. This shift occurs because static map layers are replaced by dynamic models that require frequent updates to reflect physical urban changes [1]. Extrapolating from current research, if replacement tools for environmental justice mapping are successfully deployed, the task of performing integrated GIS analyses to address scientific problems [2] may become more standardized around these new methodological benchmarks [3]. Reviewing existing or incoming data for currency and accuracy [2] will likely persist, as government-provided open-access models must still be validated against site-specific local observations [1].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, for technologists in contexts with mature digital twin infrastructures and standardized public-sector tools, the primary technical challenge shifts from data acquisition to the curation and validation of high-frequency model updates.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For technologists in regions utilizing these digital twins and standardized mapping frameworks, the long-term trajectory depends on the resolution of the tension between open-access standards and proprietary data silos. If open-access models become the universal substrate, the task of producing data layers [2] may evolve into managing real-time data streams that automatically update the 3D environment. However, a rival outcome exists where proprietary constraints limit the utility of open models, forcing technologists to continue performing manual conversion of other sources of digital data [2] to bridge incompatible systems. It remains unknown whether real-time sensor integration will eventually eliminate the need for human review of data accuracy. Meeting with clients to discuss technical specifications [2] will likely resist change, as the conceptual goals of urban planning and environmental justice remain human-directed.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, for technologists in open-data regions, the role evolves into the management of automated, real-time synchronization between physical cities and their digital twins.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, persistent data fragmentation forces technologists to remain specialized in the manual translation and conversion of incompatible proprietary spatial datasets.*

title: Document Management Specialists
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For document management specialists broadly, the introduction of specialized AI models for detecting and redacting personally identifiable information may alter how they identify and classify documents according to security levels [4]. Because PII redaction is shifting toward automated model deployment, the task of managing metadata and security characteristics may move toward the oversight of these filters [4]. In organizations using integrated cloud storage, the adoption of intelligence layers may change how they implement electronic document processing and retrieval systems, shifting them from static repositories to active collaboration tools [3]. The transition from paper markups to digital annotations requires specialists to revise how they administer document and system access rights and revision control to ensure the integrity of master documents [2]. For a subset of workers in manufacturing settings, the use of AI-translation technology may alter the process of preparing and recording changes to official documents by accelerating the synchronization of records across multilingual teams [1]. For a subset of workers managing institutional knowledge, the deployment of AI agents to mine audio meetings may alter how they identify and classify documents by automatically converting unstructured audio into searchable records [5]. However, conducting needs assessments to identify document management requirements is unlikely to change in the near term because this task depends on the specific physical and organizational constraints of end-user environments [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, the occupation may shift toward managing automated PII redaction and digital annotation workflows broadly, while subsets of workers in manufacturing and institutional knowledge management may partially automate the versioning and indexing of unstructured data.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For document management specialists broadly, if current trajectories in AI-integrated storage hold, the task of implementing electronic document processing systems may shift toward managing self-organizing information ecosystems [3]. The mechanism driving this is the evolution of storage platforms into active intelligence layers that automate retrieval and distribution without manual indexing [3]. For a subset of workers in manufacturing, extrapolating from the adoption of AI translation, the task of monitoring regulatory activity may shift toward auditing automated translation pipelines to ensure that legal and technical nuances remain compliant across different languages [1]. Despite these changes, documenting technical functions and specifications for content management systems will likely persist because system architectures remain complex and require human-authored records for disaster recovery and audit purposes [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the role may transition from managing static records toward the oversight of autonomous retrieval systems and the auditing of automated translation pipelines.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For document management specialists broadly, the future of the role may diverge based on the evolution of digital provenance. One plausible outcome is that the development of document or content classification taxonomies becomes largely autonomous, shifting the specialist's role toward the high-level policy governance of these systems. A rival outcome is that the prevalence of AI-generated alterations necessitates a return to rigid, human-certified records, increasing the specialist's role as a legal custodian of authenticity. It remains unknown whether global standards for electronic records will unify or further fragment across regulatory regimes. The requirement to implement procedures for the secure destruction of electronic records will likely resist change due to the persistent nature of statutory retention mandates and legal liability [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the specialist may shift toward high-level policy governance of autonomous classification systems.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the specialist may evolve into a legal custodian of authenticity for certified human-authored records.*

title: Penetration Testers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For penetration testers broadly, the deployment of frontier cybersecurity models such as Claude Mythos and Project Glasswing alters the task to identify security system weaknesses by automating the discovery of zero-day vulnerabilities in open-source software [15][53][69] and legacy server software [23]. Because adversaries now utilize AI-native vectors—including indirect prompt injection [81][92], agentic memory attacks [32][79], and prompt injection resulting in remote code execution [50]—testers must integrate these mechanisms when they identify new threat tactics, techniques, or procedures [2]. The emergence of AI-assisted supply chain attacks [5] and the exploitation of non-human identities [12] changes the requirements for those who develop infiltration tests that exploit device vulnerabilities [2]. In organizations using cloud-native infrastructure, frontier agents may automate specific portions of security testing and cloud operations workflows [1]. For a subset of workers in the automotive sector, automated V2G security testing streamlines the task to test the security of systems within networked vehicle environments [33]. The task to assess the physical security of servers, systems, or network devices is unlikely to change because it requires manual, on-site hardware verification [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, penetration testers will integrate autonomous vulnerability discovery and AI-native attack vectors into their workflows, while specialists in cloud and automotive sectors adopt domain-specific agents for simulation.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For penetration testers broadly, if current trajectories in autonomous vulnerability mapping hold, the task to identify security system weaknesses may shift from manual discovery to the verification and auditing of complex attack paths generated by large-scale AI initiatives [101]. Extrapolating from trends in red team workflow automation and the development of autonomous systems like PentAGI and Scenario, the task to gather cyber intelligence to identify vulnerabilities could be partially managed by orchestration platforms that standardize the reconnaissance process [3][57][70]. For testers working in financial institutions, the role may shift toward validating risk briefs provided by regulators regarding AI-driven cyber risks [28][31][43][93]. For a subset of testers operating in the bug bounty market, the economic model could be constrained by AI-led remediation cycles that close vulnerabilities before human researchers can report them [19]. However, the task to write audit reports to communicate technical and procedural findings persists as a human-led activity because the attribution of risk and alignment with organizational business logic require human accountability [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, technical exploitation may shift toward the auditing of autonomous AI-led attack chains, while formal reporting and regulatory validation remain human-centric due to accountability constraints.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For penetration testers broadly, the long-term status of the task to test the security of systems depends on whether AI agents achieve a stable capacity to discover novel architectural vulnerabilities without human-defined heuristics. A primary uncertainty remains whether the iterative cycle between AI-led discovery and AI-led remediation results in a stable security baseline or a state of permanent volatility. One plausible outcome is the total automation of the technical exploit chain, shifting the human role to the strategic orchestration of multi-vector campaigns and the management of agent-first governance [52]. A rival outcome is that the efficiency of AI-driven exploitation forces a regression to hardware-based security and air-gapped environments for critical systems, rendering the traditional network-based penetration test obsolete for high-security enclaves. The task to discuss security solutions with information technology teams or management resists complete automation because it involves negotiating organizational risk appetites and resource allocation [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation evolves into a strategic oversight role focused on the orchestration of autonomous agent swarms and the governance of AI-led defense-offense cycles.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the extreme volatility of AI-driven exploits renders software-based testing secondary to the physical auditing of air-gapped and hardware-isolated systems.*

title: Information Security Engineers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For information security engineers broadly, the proliferation of residential proxies used to mask attack traffic renders IP-based reputation systems ineffective, shifting the task of develop or install software to protect sensitive information toward identity-centric verification and zero-trust architectures [5][93]. To identify security system weaknesses, engineers must implement kernel-level protections to counter "bring your own vulnerable driver" (BYOVD) techniques that allow ransomware to disable endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools [6][36]. The rise of unmanaged non-human identities and orphaned API keys alters the task of identify or implement solutions to information security problems by requiring the design of automated discovery and rotation systems for service accounts [14][43][47][56][93], including the use of secret managers to decouple workloads from sensitive credentials [91]. For a subset of workers managing AI agent integrations, the emergence of prompt-injection vectors achieving remote code execution (RCE) and agentic memory attacks shifts the task of coordinate monitoring of networks or systems for security breaches toward auditing AI-agent session-crossing data leaks and sandbox escapes [13][31][50][52][54][55][60][76][80][89], utilizing specialized governance toolkits for non-human identity oversight [18][22][24][84] and implementing safeguards for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines [100]. For engineers in critical infrastructure settings, targeted attacks on PLC and SCADA systems shift the task of identify security system weaknesses toward the hardening of operational technology and signal verification [12][16][46][81]. In regions implementing universal device identity, as reported in India, the task of develop or install software to protect sensitive information may shift toward building technical infrastructure for device-level digital identities [75]. The failure of one-time passwords (OTPs) against adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing shifts the task of develop or install software toward implementing session binding and continuous authentication [17][70][99]. To address the "zero-window" era where patching latency exceeds attack speed, the task of develop response and recovery strategies for security breaches shifts toward the deployment of network detection and response (NDR) systems for immediate containment [101]. The manual verification of physical hardware seals on air-gapped servers is unlikely to change, as these protocols rely on physical tamper-evidence rather than digital signals [72].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, information security engineers will transition from IP-based perimeter defenses toward identity-centric controls and kernel-level hardening, while implementing specialized lifecycle management for non-human identities and agentic AI sandboxes.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For information security engineers broadly, if high-capability cybersecurity models transition from limited preview to general operational deployment, the task of identify security system weaknesses may shift from manual execution toward overseeing automated vulnerability discovery and remediation loops [9][34][40][42][59][92]. Extrapolating from current agentic attack speeds, the task of coordinate monitoring of networks or systems for security breaches could shift toward the orchestration of autonomous defense agents designed to match the latency of agentic attackers [11][39][62][64][82][103]. For a subset of workers managing high-sensitivity data, the emergence of quantum computing threats may shift the task of develop or install software to protect sensitive information toward the implementation of post-quantum cryptographic standards [26][41]. The development of information security standards and best practices will likely persist as a human-led task due to the need for alignment with evolving legal frameworks and organizational risk appetites.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupation may shift from manual vulnerability management toward the orchestration of autonomous AI-driven defense agents and the deployment of quantum-resistant encryption.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For information security engineers broadly, the long-term trajectory remains uncertain due to the potential for an "agentic equilibrium" where offensive and defensive AI capabilities reach a stalemate. One possible outcome is the shift of the task of troubleshoot security and network problems toward the management of high-level strategic intent for autonomous security swarms, while the underlying technical execution is fully abstracted. A rival outcome involves a retreat from complex software dependencies toward hardware-defined security and air-gapped architectures if AI-driven software fragility becomes systemic. The exact timing and efficacy of quantum-safe transitions remain a primary unknown. The requirement for forensic investigation of security breaches will likely resist full automation, as legal attribution and evidentiary standards for court proceedings require human-verified chains of custody.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation evolves into a strategic oversight role, managing autonomous security ecosystems that operate at speeds beyond human perception.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, software-based security is deemed too fragile, forcing a return to hardware-centric isolation and physical security primitives.*

title: Digital Forensics Analysts
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For digital forensics analysts broadly, the prevalence of high-fidelity synthetic media alters the task to perform file signature analysis to require the integration of automated provenance verification to distinguish biological captures from AI-manipulated hybrids [3][19][24][30]. Because agentic AI can now task humans as unsuspecting accomplices, the task to analyze log files or other digital information to identify the perpetrators of network intrusions now requires methods to trace the chain of command from human actions back to autonomous agent logs [36]. The emergence of AI-mediated "ghost breach" narratives requires the task to write technical summaries to report findings to include the explicit disproof of fabricated security incidents [12]. For a subset of workers investigating macOS endpoints, home routers, or corporate collaboration platforms, the use of ClickFix, Mirai variants, GopherWhisper, and the SNOW malware suite necessitates updated scripts to automate tasks and the development of new reverse-engineering tools to identify persistence mechanisms [1][10][14][21][25][28][29][32][34]. In US regulatory settings, the tasks to perform forensic investigations of operating or file systems may now include the analysis of LLM prompt histories [17], while the task to adhere to legal policies involves navigating shifting legal standards for geofence warrants [33]. For a subset of workers specializing in blockchain intelligence, the task to analyze log files is being assisted by AI models designed to track illicit cryptocurrency transactions [35]. The task to recover data or decrypt seized data is constrained by rapid vendor security updates that block access to specific data streams, such as push notifications on iOS [22]. The task to adhere to legal policies and procedures related to handling digital media is unlikely to change because judicial requirements for chain-of-custody remain structurally independent of the technical methods used to capture evidence [22].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, forensic verification workflows will integrate synthetic media detection and the reconstruction of agent-human command chains as standard components of evidence validation.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For digital forensics analysts broadly, if current trajectories of AI-driven fraud and synthetic identity proliferation hold, the task to conduct predictive or reactive analyses on security measures may transition toward detecting longitudinal behavioral anomalies rather than static actor signatures [4][9][18]. The deployment of specialized defensive models, such as GPT-5.4-Cyber, could automate the initial triage and pattern-recognition phases of the task to analyze log files [11][13]. However, the requirement to write reports, sign affidavits, or give depositions for legal proceedings persists unchanged because the erosion of digital trust increases the necessity for human expert attestation to satisfy legal standards of evidence [3][8]. This transition remains conditional on the development of telemetry capable of distinguishing biological human behavior from high-fidelity AI simulations. The task to maintain knowledge of laws, regulations, policies or other issuances is unlikely to change significantly as the core legal principles of evidence admissibility evolve more slowly than the underlying technical capabilities [22].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, attribution efforts will rely more on long-term behavioral baselining and less on isolated technical signatures to identify perpetrators of network intrusions.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For digital forensics analysts broadly, the scope of investigation may expand to include the forensic auditing of autonomous agent goals and objective functions to determine intent in computer-based crimes. One major uncertainty remains whether adversarial AI can produce perfectly indistinguishable synthetic logs that render traditional file system forensics obsolete. The task to preserve and maintain digital forensic evidence for analysis will likely resist change, as the physical isolation of evidence remains a fundamental requirement for legal admissibility.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, digital forensics shifts toward "algorithmic archaeology," focusing on the reconstruction of AI decision-trees and objective-function shifts to establish legal culpability.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the ubiquity of perfect synthetic evidence leads to a collapse of symbolic digital forensics, forcing a return to hardware-level physical telemetry as the only reliable source of truth.*

title: Blockchain Engineers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For the occupation broadly, increasing evidence of quantum vulnerabilities may shift the criteria used to design and verify cryptographic protocols to protect private information [3]. For a subset of engineers managing high-throughput ecosystems, the development of specific migration paths may alter how they design and deploy blockchain design patterns to mitigate future quantum threats [7]. For workers in the TON ecosystem, the launch of agentic wallets and specialized compute stacks may require them to design and develop blockchain technologies specifically for autonomous AI agents [8]. For a subset of engineers managing open-source repositories on GitHub, the prevalence of token giveaway scams may shift how they assess blockchain threats, specifically regarding the protection of keys [1]. In regulated banking settings in Switzerland, the testing of sovereign stablecoins may increase the focus on designing and deploy blockchain design patterns to ensure transaction immutability for pegged assets [2]. In the European Union, the adoption of ECB payment standards may shift how a subset of engineers design and develop blockchain technologies for finance to ensure compliance with digital euro regulations [5][6]. For engineers in the U.S. fintech subsegment, the PACE Act may require them to update client and server applications to integrate decentralized ledgers with centralized Federal Reserve payment rails [4]. The task of automating the deployment of software updates over geographically distributed network nodes is unlikely to change, as node orchestration remains functionally independent of the underlying cryptographic primitives [2][6].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, blockchain engineering will be characterized by a shift toward quantum-resistant cryptographic evaluation, the integration of decentralized ledgers into sovereign payment systems, and the creation of specialized financial infrastructure for autonomous AI agents.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For the occupation broadly, if current trajectories hold, the transition from research to operational deployment of quantum-safe security protocols may shift the core requirement to design and verify cryptographic protocols [3][7]. For engineers in regulated banking settings in Switzerland and the European Union, extrapolating from current regional tests, the task of designing and developing blockchain technologies for finance may shift toward the creation of interoperable, quantum-resistant sovereign digital currency standards [2][5][6]. For engineers in the TON ecosystem and similar agentic environments, the proliferation of AI-driven transactions may alter how they design and implement data repositories to integrate agent-to-agent payment logs [8]. For those in U.S. fintech settings, the integration of private ledgers with centralized rails may alter how they discuss and plan systems with solution architects to meet liquidity and regulatory requirements [4]. The requirement to discuss data needs with engineers, product managers, or data scientists to identify blockchain requirements remains unchanged, as these coordination tasks are driven by organizational logic rather than technological shifts [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupation may bifurcate into specialized roles focused on the interoperability of sovereign digital assets, defensive security engineers maintaining post-quantum networks, and infrastructure engineers specializing in autonomous agentic economies.*

## Far (2046–2051)

Scope remains limited to the broader occupation and the specific financial, agentic, and open-source settings established in the near term. Rival outcomes exist regarding whether the transition to quantum-safe cryptography is completed across all legacy networks or if specific high-value chains are abandoned due to migration failures. A primary uncertainty is the exact timing and capability of quantum computers to break elliptic curve cryptography, which dictates the urgency and method of redesigning cryptographic protocols [3]. The necessity to implement catastrophic failure handlers to identify security breaches and prevent serious damage resists change even at this horizon, as the error cost of digital asset loss remains catastrophic regardless of the underlying ledger technology.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, blockchain engineering may converge into a standardized utility role focused on maintaining a global, quantum-safe ledger layer integrated into sovereign financial rails.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation may fragment into highly isolated, proprietary ledger environments where security is maintained through closed-loop licensing and restrictive access rather than open cryptographic protocols.*

title: Computer Systems Engineers/Architects
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For computer systems architects broadly, establishing functional or system standards now incorporates cost per token as the primary metric for calculating total cost of ownership [10]. Developing system architectures requires integrating specialized AI model customization pipelines to address performance gaps in base models [1], treating AI agents as internal software components rather than external service entities [27], and creating orchestration frameworks to mitigate agent sprawl within enterprise environments [16]. Identifying system data, hardware, or software components now includes specifying gigawatt-scale power and cooling infrastructure for massive compute clusters [9], selecting tensor processing units specifically designed for agentic workloads [17], and prioritizing data path and movement efficiency over peak compute throughput [32]. Additionally, architects must now evaluate current or emerging technologies to mitigate the budget and operational constraints imposed by AI vendor lock-in [30]. For a subset of architects designing agentic systems, identifying hardware components is shifting focus from GPU-centricity toward increased CPU and memory capacity [14][21]. In these same agentic contexts, directing the analysis and operation of complete computer systems requires the implementation of risk intelligence frameworks to manage the non-deterministic behavior of autonomous agent fleets [2][15]. For architects in regions prioritizing infrastructure autonomy, developing distributed system architectures involves the construction of massive card-based computing clusters [7], while those in regions implementing sovereign AI initiatives focus on designing supercomputing systems that prioritize reduced capital expenditure [11]. For a subset of workers managing enterprise modernization, evaluating existing systems involves designing AI-native infrastructure to integrate legacy mainframe data via agentic layers [20]. In high-performance inference settings, verifying the scalability of system architecture involves implementing tensor, context, and expert parallelism [4] and utilizing optimized GPU communication protocols on non-proprietary platforms [3]. For architects in data center procurement, evaluating emerging technologies includes assessing open-standard AI chips to reduce physical hardware footprints [5][8] and incorporating LPDDR6 updates for non-mobile AI platforms [25]. In specific cloud-provisioning contexts, configuring servers includes the deployment of specialized instances, such as G7e nodes, to accelerate generative AI inference [13]. For architects in hyperscale cloud consumer organizations, configuring servers requires redesigning architecture to scale across massive ARM-based CPU-core counts [22][23][29]. For architects managing power allocation, completing models and simulations now involves using rapid estimation methods to forecast AI power consumption [28] and addressing AI-driven utility load planning constraints [24]. The task of communicating with staff or clients to understand specific system requirements is unlikely to change yet, as the translation of ambiguous business goals into technical constraints remains a high-context human negotiation [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, the occupation's core focus shifts from general resource virtualization to the optimization of inference-specific hardware and the architectural containment of autonomous agent deployments.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For a subset of architects in organizations adopting AI-native stacks, evaluating existing systems will likely shift from incremental patching to the complete replacement of legacy architectures with systems designed for agentic orchestration, if current trajectories in legacy migration hold [20]. Extrapolating from current procurement trends, investigating system component suitability may move toward the prioritization of data movement efficiency over raw compute throughput, as the architectural bottleneck shifts from computation to interconnects [32]. If the cost-per-token metric remains the dominant TCO driver, establishing system standards may increasingly favor architectures that optimize for energy-efficient inference over massive training capacity [10]. The task of directing the installation of operating systems is unlikely to change in its fundamental purpose, as the requirement for low-level hardware initialization remains a prerequisite for any higher-level system abstraction.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the architectural role may shift from managing general-purpose compute resources to orchestrating highly specialized, data-movement-optimized "AI factories" tailored for specific token-cost targets.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For computer systems architects broadly, the architectural focus may diverge between two competing paradigms. One scenario involves the dominance of hyper-centralized, gigawatt-scale AI hubs where identifying hardware components is driven by extreme scale and specialized cooling [9]. A rival scenario involves the proliferation of extremely efficient, local agentic hardware, where developing system architectures centers on deploying models on ubiquitous, non-GPU neural processing units [6][26]. A key uncertainty remains whether new silicon paradigms or energy-harvesting technologies will collapse the distinction between these two scales. Even at this horizon, verifying stability, interoperability, and security of system architecture will resist change, as these remain the non-negotiable constraints of any production-grade system.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation evolves into the management of a few global-scale, energy-dense compute monoliths that serve as the primary architectural anchors for all AI services.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation shifts toward the design of hyper-distributed, heterogeneous architectures where agentic intelligence is embedded in a vast array of low-power, localized hardware.*

title: Information Technology Project Managers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For IT project managers broadly, the adoption of continuous discovery and adaptive development in AI-integrated environments may shift the task to *monitor or track project milestones* from tracking fixed roadmaps to managing real-time feedback loops [4]. This shift occurs because the iterative nature of AI deployment renders traditional, static product roadmaps less effective for coordinating technical delivery [4]. For a subset of workers overseeing AI initiatives in cloud environments, the task to *develop or update project plans* may incorporate "path-to-value" frameworks to align technical output with specific business outcomes [3]. In this same subsegment, the task to *develop and manage annual budgets* is being modified by tools that attribute specific inference costs to individual workloads, replacing broad estimates with granular financial data [2]. Additionally, the task to *perform risk assessments* must now account for a documented "execution gap" where approximately half of AI projects miss targets despite high organizational optimism [1]. The task to *negotiate with project stakeholders* is unlikely to change because aligning divergent business priorities requires human social mediation and political navigation [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, IT project managers will increasingly move from milestone-based tracking toward adaptive iteration, while those in AI subsegments will integrate granular cost-tracking and value-delivery frameworks to mitigate a persistent execution gap.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For IT project managers broadly, if current trajectories in adaptive development hold, the task to *submit project deliverables* may shift toward verifying continuous value creation metrics rather than mere technical completion [4]. For the subsegment of AI project managers, extrapolating from the existing execution gap, the task to *confer with project personnel to identify and resolve problems* will persist as a primary manual activity [1]. This persistence is due to the fact that execution failures in AI are often rooted in organizational governance and legacy constraints rather than technical tooling [1]. The core requirement to *direct or coordinate activities of project personnel* remains a human-led function because counteracting systemic over-optimism requires nuanced leadership and psychological safety [1].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupation may shift toward value-driven delivery oversight, though human-led problem resolution remains critical for the AI subsegment to navigate organizational governance failures.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For IT project managers broadly, the long-term structural change depends on whether adaptive iteration becomes the universal standard or if high-risk environments return to rigid roadmaps for stability. For the AI-focused subsegment, one plausible outcome is that the execution gap narrows as automated risk-response strategies integrate with real-time cost and performance telemetry, potentially automating the task to *prepare project status reports* [1][2][3]. A rival outcome suggests that the increasing interdependence of non-deterministic AI systems creates unpredictable failure modes, ensuring that the task to *manage project execution* remains heavily dependent on human intervention [1]. It remains unknown whether the "execution gap" is a temporary artifact of early adoption or a systemic property of AI deployment. The task to *assess current or future customer needs* resists change even at this horizon because the definition of strategic "value" remains a subjective negotiation between human stakeholders [3].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the integration of structured value frameworks and real-time telemetry may effectively eliminate the execution gap for AI-centric projects.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the systemic complexity of interdependent AI systems may render the execution gap a permanent feature, maintaining the necessity of human-centric project steering.*

title: Actuaries
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For actuaries broadly, the emergence of unpredictability in automated internal processes is introducing a new class of volatility that complicates the determination of insurable risk. As insurance carriers decline to cover certain AI outputs [1], actuaries must adjust how they construct probability tables for events involving systemic technical failure [O*NET 6]. This shift requires actuaries to ascertain premium rates and cash reserves specifically for the risk of AI-induced operational loss [O*NET 1]. Because the distribution of AI failure events is not yet historically documented, the initial approach focuses on quantifying the volatility and unpredictability of these outputs to determine if they are mathematically insurable [1]. The core analysis of biological mortality and sickness rates is unlikely to change in this period, as these are driven by physiological factors independent of the software architectures currently causing insurance retreats.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, actuaries will prioritize the development of volatility frameworks to define the boundaries of insurable AI risk.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For actuaries broadly, if current trajectories of risk aversion persist, the occupation may shift toward creating specialized risk-weighting frameworks based on the specific architecture of a client's AI systems. Extrapolating from the current trend of carriers backing away from general AI outputs [1], actuaries may be required to provide expertise to financial institutions to maximize returns while managing the specific "tail risk" associated with AI dependencies [O*NET 10]. This would involve integrating technical telemetry—such as error rates and drift metrics—into the probability tables used to forecast liability [O*NET 6]. The fundamental requirement to maintain cash reserves to ensure payment of future benefits remains unchanged, as this is a solvency mandate that exists regardless of the risk source [O*NET 1].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, actuarial models may incorporate real-time system performance data to calibrate premiums for AI-driven operational risks.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For actuaries broadly, the long-term status of AI risk depends on whether failure patterns become predictable or remain systemic. One possibility is that AI failure becomes a standardized risk class with stable probability tables, similar to natural disasters [O*NET 6]. A competing outcome is that the high correlation of failures across different companies using the same foundational models creates a "systemic collapse" scenario that is mathematically uninsurable. The exact distribution of these "fat-tail" events remains an unresolvable uncertainty at this horizon. Despite these shifts, the basic mathematical process of using statistical data to forecast liability persists, as the laws of probability remain constant even as the objects of observation change.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, AI-related operational risk is fully commoditized and integrated into standard actuarial probability tables.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the systemic nature of AI failure renders such risks uninsurable, shifting the liability from the private insurance market to state-backed guarantee funds.*


## References

title: Mathematicians
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subset of mathematicians working in formal methods and theoretical computer science, experimental workflows may incorporate automated systems converting informal textbook text into formal proofs. This mechanism affects the task of developing new principles and new relationships between existing mathematical principles by reducing labor required to verify existing knowledge [1]. The task of disseminating research may shift toward including formalized versions alongside traditional papers in specific journals [2]. However, the task of assembling sets of assumptions and exploring the consequences of each set remains largely human-dependent due to the ambiguity of informal mathematical intuition. Widespread adoption across all mathematical subfields is unlikely in this period due to the specialized nature of formal verification tools.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, experimental workflows in formal mathematics may incorporate automated verification tools, while broader practice remains unchanged.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For the same subset of workers in formal methods, if current trajectories hold, automated verification could become a standard checkpoint for published proofs. This extends the task of conducting research to include formal validation steps before submission [1]. The task of maintaining knowledge in the field may involve curating formal libraries rather than just reading professional journals [2]. However, the core task of developing new principles to advance mathematical science resists full automation because novelty requires insight beyond pattern matching.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, formal verification may become a routine step for specific subfields, but human insight drives principle development.*

## Far (2046–2051)

In the far term, rival outcomes emerge regarding the language of mathematical communication within this subset. One outcome suggests formalization becomes mandatory for high-stakes proofs, while a competing view suggests formalization remains a niche tool for verification only. The task of addressing the relationships of quantities, magnitudes, and forms through the use of numbers and symbols remains resistant to full change because mathematical intuition is deeply embedded in informal notation.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, formalized proofs may become the primary standard for verification in specific domains.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, informal notation remains dominant for communication, with formal tools serving only as backend checks.*
