title: First-Line Supervisors of Food Preparation and Serving Workers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For first-line supervisors broadly, the adoption of integrated management software may alter how they perform tasks related to controlling inventories of food [1] and analyzing operational problems, such as theft and wastage [1]. These tools automate cost management and waste tracking, shifting the supervisor's role from manual data collection to the review of software-generated reports [1]. For a subset of supervisors in organizations implementing performance-linked bonuses for front-line staff, the process of observing and evaluating workers [2] may shift toward monitoring the specific key performance indicators (KPIs) required to trigger payouts [3]. Additionally, the task of training workers in food preparation [2] may be partially offloaded to integrated digital training portals [1]. The task of resolving customer complaints regarding food service [2] is unlikely to change, as it requires real-time emotional intelligence and situational judgment to manage dissatisfied guests.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, supervisors broadly may rely on integrated software to automate inventory and waste analysis, while those in bonus-incentivized organizations may shift toward metric-driven worker evaluation.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For supervisors broadly, if the trajectory of integrated management software continues, the task of analyzing operational problems [2] may shift from descriptive reporting to prescriptive intervention based on software-driven benchmarks [1]. Extrapolating from current incentive models, supervisors in organizations using performance bonuses may find that the evaluation of workers [2] becomes increasingly reliant on automated KPI dashboards, reducing the frequency of subjective supervisory observations [3]. The task of assigning duties, responsibilities, and work stations to employees [2] will likely persist as a manual coordination activity due to the high physical variability of customer flow and staffing gaps in food service environments.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, supervisors broadly may adopt prescriptive software for cost and waste management, while worker evaluation in specific incentive-driven settings may become more automated.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For supervisors broadly and those in incentive-driven organizations, the long-term evolution of the role depends on the degree to which "supervision" is defined as technical oversight versus interpersonal management. If inventory, cost management, and training tasks are fully offloaded to autonomous systems, the supervisory role may consolidate around resolving customer complaints [2] and managing high-stakes interpersonal conflicts. Conversely, if the use of rigid software for waste and performance metrics creates systemic worker friction or burnout, supervisors may be forced to shift their focus toward intensive personnel support and retention strategies to maintain operational capacity [3]. The task of inspecting supplies, equipment, and work areas to ensure conformance to standards [2] resists change, as health and safety regulations generally require a physical human presence to verify sanitation.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the supervisory role may evolve into a primarily interpersonal and conflict-resolution position as technical oversight is automated.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, supervisors may shift toward high-touch personnel support to counteract the friction caused by algorithmic management.*

title: Cooks, Fast Food
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For fast food cooks in high-wage regulatory regions and those in organizations adopting autonomous kitchen systems, the stability of the role is subject to divergent pressures. In regions with high minimum wage mandates, such as California, increased labor costs for core tasks like operating large-volume cooking equipment [2] may result in business insolvency for some franchisees [1]. Simultaneously, in a subsegment of the industry, the deployment of retrofitted autonomous systems may begin to replace the task of cooking and packaging batches of food [2]. Because these robotic systems are designed for specific, limited-menu items, the task of preparing specialty foods [2] that require nuanced manual assembly is unlikely to change for most workers in the near term. Manual cleaning of food preparation areas and utensils [2] persists as a human requirement due to the high variability of kitchen grime and the complexity of sanitation verification.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, cooks in high-wage regions may face increased employment instability, while those in automating subsegments may see a reduction in batch-cooking tasks.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

Within these same high-wage regions and automating subsegments, if current trajectories of labor cost increases and robotic retrofitting hold, the requirement for human labor to cook the exact number of items ordered by each customer [2] may decrease. Extrapolating from the current ability to retrofit existing kitchens [2], the mechanism of change is the gradual replacement of human-operated grills and fryers with autonomous modules to lower per-unit labor costs [1]. However, the responsibility to maintain sanitation, health, and safety standards in work areas [2] is likely to remain a human-centric task because of the high error cost associated with foodborne illness and the difficulty of automating deep-cleaning protocols.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, labor-cost pressures and the availability of retrofitted automation may shift the cook's role away from active food preparation toward system monitoring in specific organizational contexts.*

## Far (2046–2051)

In high-wage regulatory environments and automated subsegments, the long-term structural survival of the human cook role remains uncertain. One plausible outcome is the near-complete automation of core cooking and packaging tasks [2], where humans are retained only to verify that prepared food meets requirements for quality and quantity [2]. A rival outcome involves a market shift where fast food operators move toward premium, higher-priced menus that justify the retention of human labor for preparing specialty foods [2]. A critical unknown is whether regulatory bodies will permit fully autonomous kitchens to operate without an on-site human licensed for food safety. Even at this horizon, the task of taking out garbage resists automation due to the unstructured nature of waste disposal environments and the physical variability of the task.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the cooking function in high-wage regions may shift almost entirely to automated systems, with humans relegated to quality oversight.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation may persist through a shift to premium pricing models that sustain human labor for specialty food preparation.*

title: Cooks, Institution and Cafeteria
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subset of workers in institutions adopting multi-functional intelligent ovens, the integration of steam, hot air, and microwave capabilities into single units may alter the process of cooking foodstuffs according to menus [1]. Because these systems coordinate different thermal methods within one piece of equipment, cooks in these settings may spend less time moving product between separate appliances [1]. This consolidation could reduce the time required to clean and inspect galley equipment [2] by decreasing the total number of independent appliances to be maintained. However, the requirement to monitor and record food temperatures [2] is unlikely to change in the near term due to strict institutional health and safety regulations regarding foodborne illness.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, a subset of institutional cooks will utilize integrated cooking technology to reduce appliance footprints and consolidate thermal processing tasks.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For the same subset of workers in high-capital institutional settings, the continued adoption of intelligent multi-functional units may shift the task of requisitioning kitchen equipment [2]. If current trajectories hold, procurement may move away from a diverse array of single-purpose tools toward fewer, more expensive integrated systems [1]. This shift could consolidate the technical skills required to operate separate microwave and steaming cycles into a single interface. The task of rotating and storing food supplies [2] will likely remain unchanged, as it depends on physical storage constraints and inventory logistics rather than cooking technology.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the reliance on single-purpose industrial appliances may decline in well-funded institutional kitchens, consolidating cooking tasks into integrated intelligent hubs.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For workers in institutions using highly integrated thermal systems, the role may diverge based on the specific institutional constraint. In settings with high volume and low variance, cooking may shift primarily toward the supervision of automated cycles [1]. Conversely, in hospitals where dietary or nutritional restrictions [2] require extreme precision and frequent adjustments, manual oversight of thermal processes may persist to mitigate the high error cost of incorrect food preparation. The physical task of apportioning and serving food to facility residents [2] remains resistant to change as it requires embodied interaction with patrons. It remains unknown whether the long-term maintenance costs of hyper-integrated equipment will eventually favor a return to simpler, modular appliances.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, cooking in high-volume institutional settings may shift primarily toward the supervision and programming of multi-functional automated systems.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the necessity of strict dietary adherence in medical institutions may maintain the requirement for manual intervention and traditional equipment oversight.*

title: Cooks, Restaurant
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subset of workers in organizations adopting integrated cooking hardware and robotic retrofits, the physical workflow of food production is consolidating. Because integrated oven technology can coordinate steam, hot air, and microwave functions within one unit, the movement of food between separate appliances to bake, roast, broil, and steam meats and vegetables is reduced [1]. Simultaneously, the deployment of robotic systems into existing kitchens may begin to automate specific core tasks, such as the need to season and cook food according to recipes [2]. This may alter the task of regulating temperature of ovens, broilers, grills, and roasters by shifting control from manual adjustment to software-defined presets [1][2]. However, the task of inspecting and cleaning food preparation areas remains unlikely to change because the physical removal of organic debris and the maintenance of sanitary standards require manual dexterity and site-specific judgment [2]. Sensory-based quality control, specifically observing and testing foods through tasting and smelling, persists as a human requirement due to the lack of organoleptic sensors in current hardware [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, workers in high-automation kitchen settings may experience a reduction in repetitive appliance-switching and a shift toward supervising automated cooking cycles.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For the same subset of workers utilizing robotic retrofits and integrated thermal systems, if current trajectories of hardware deployment hold, the execution of routine cooking motions may become more autonomous. Extrapolating from the integration of robotic systems into existing kitchens, the manual requirement to turn or stir foods to ensure even cooking and the need to weigh, measure, and mix ingredients may decrease as automated actuators handle these repetitive tasks [2]. The precision of integrated sensors may further reduce the frequency of manual interventions required to regulate temperature [1]. Despite these shifts, the task of washing, peeling, cutting, and seeding fruits and vegetables is likely to persist as a human-led activity because of the high variability in the shape and texture of raw produce [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the physical labor associated with routine ingredient processing and heat management may decrease for workers in robotically retrofitted kitchens.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For workers in these specialized high-automation environments, the occupation may diverge based on the economic value assigned to manual craft. One plausible outcome involves the near-total automation of the cooking phase, where the worker's role shifts primarily to the peripheral tasks of portioning, arranging, and garnishing food [2]. A rival outcome involves a market shift toward "analog" cooking in premium settings, where the ability to season and cook food according to personal judgment and experience—independent of integrated intelligence—becomes the primary marker of occupational value [2]. It remains unknown whether synthetic sensory technology will ever allow machines to perform the task of tasting and smelling for doneness [2]. Even in high-automation scenarios, the task of butchering and dressing animals or carving and trimming meats will likely resist change due to the complex, non-standardized anatomy of biological materials [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the role in high-tech kitchens may transition into a supervisory and plating function, where the cooking phase is a bounded-autonomy system.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, a premium on human judgment may preserve the traditional requirement for manual seasoning and temperature control in high-value culinary settings.*

title: Food Preparation Workers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subset of workers in high-volume or corporate kitchen settings, the adoption of retrofitted automation tools may reduce the manual burden of repetitive preparation [1]. Because robotic systems can be integrated into existing kitchen layouts to handle ingredient preparation and basic assembly, the time spent to wash, peel, and cut various foods may decrease [1]. Similarly, the use of manual or electric appliances to clean, peel, slice, and trim foods could be partially shifted to autonomous units in these specific settings [1]. Tasks involving the assembly of meal trays may also see a transition toward robotic assistance in standardized environments [1]. However, tasks requiring high mobility in unstructured environments, such as removing trash and cleaning kitchen garbage containers, are unlikely to change because of the current limitations in autonomous waste navigation and handling [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, automation will likely be confined to a subsegment of workers in standardized, high-volume environments, reducing the manual time spent on ingredient preparation and basic assembly.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For the same subset of workers in automated corporate or high-volume settings, if current trajectories in retrofitting hold, automation may extend to more complex portioning and mixing tasks [1]. Extrapolating from current deployment patterns, the task to portion and wrap food could be further delegated to autonomous systems as precision in handling diverse textures improves [1]. The mechanism of modular robotic integration may also allow for the automation of mixing ingredients for green salads and other cold dishes [2]. Despite these shifts, the task to assist cooks and kitchen staff with various tasks as needed will likely persist, as this requires real-time, unpredictable responsiveness to human instructions that exceeds the capabilities of current task-specific automation [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the scope of automation within high-volume settings may expand to include portioning and cold-food mixing, provided robotic dexterity continues to improve.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For workers in high-volume settings, the potential for further automation depends on the resolution of the tension between operational efficiency and quality perception. One plausible outcome is that nearly all repetitive prep tasks, including butchering and cleaning fowl, fish, poultry, and shellfish, become automated in corporate contexts [2]. A competing outcome is that a demand for artisanal, human-led preparation creates a permanent divide in the occupation, where human workers are retained specifically for high-end or specialized preparation to maintain a "hand-crafted" value proposition. It remains unknown whether the error costs associated with food safety and cross-contamination will be more effectively managed by autonomous systems or human oversight. Regardless of the outcome, the requirement to clean and sanitize work areas and equipment will likely remain a human-led or human-supervised task due to the critical nature of health regulation compliance [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, repetitive preparation tasks in high-volume settings may be almost entirely automated, shifting the remaining human role toward system oversight and sanitation compliance.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation may bifurcate, with automation dominating corporate settings while human preparation is preserved in high-end settings as a mark of quality.*

title: Bartenders
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For bartenders broadly, consumer tipping fatigue may reduce the frequency and volume of gratuities processed during the task of collecting money for drinks served [1]. For bartenders in the United States, revised IRS deduction rules may alter the administrative recording and reporting requirements involved in balancing cash receipts [2]. In specific urban municipalities like Chicago that are phasing out tip credits, the mechanism for calculating base hourly wages relative to gratuities is shifting [3][4]. For bartenders in conflict-affected regions, such as those in Cairo, state-mandated early closures of nightlife establishments may restrict the ability to plan, organize, and control the operations of a cocktail lounge or bar [5]. The task of checking identification of customers to verify age requirements is unlikely to change because it is governed by binding legal mandates and liquor licensing regimes [2]. Similarly, the physical process of mixing ingredients to prepare cocktails remains stable as it relies on established recipe standards and manual dexterity [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, bartenders may experience a decline in discretionary earnings and increased regional variability in wage structures and operating hours due to shifting consumer behaviors, local regulations, and geopolitical instability.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For bartenders broadly, if current trajectories of tipping fatigue persist, the mechanism for collecting money for drinks served may shift toward structured service charges or modified payment models to stabilize labor income [1]. This shift would occur because a reliance on discretionary gratuities may become an insufficient incentive for labor retention in high-fatigue consumer environments [1]. Such a transition would depend on the ability of establishments to implement service fees without alienating price-sensitive patrons [1]. The task of stocking the bar with beer, wine, liquor, and related supplies is unlikely to change because it depends on low-cost manual coordination and the existing physical architecture of bar layouts [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the compensation structure for bartenders may move away from discretionary tipping toward more stabilized, organization-led payment mechanisms.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For bartenders broadly, the economic model of the occupation may diverge based on the service environment. In one scenario, the role could transition to a standardized wage model as discretionary tipping ceases to be a viable primary income source across most settings [1][3][4]. In a competing scenario, tipping may persist exclusively in luxury settings where gratuities function as a social signal of status rather than a standard service fee [1]. It remains unknown whether tax frameworks for digital payments and tip deductions [2] will evolve into a global standard or remain fragmented by jurisdiction. The task of attempting to limit problems and liability related to customers' excessive drinking will likely resist change because it requires real-time social perceptiveness and the management of unpredictable human behavior [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may shift toward a standardized hourly wage model across most service settings.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation may bifurcate into a market where tipping survives only in high-end, luxury environments.*

title: Fast Food and Counter Workers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subset of workers in drive-thru and convenience store settings, the deployment of voice AI agents is automating the task of requesting and recording customer orders [3][4][5][8]. For the occupation broadly, the adoption of AI-powered ordering platforms is shifting the mechanism of order entry from static digital menus toward interactive interfaces that assist customers in menu navigation [6]. In regions where mandatory minimum wages create high financial pressure on franchisees, such as in California, this automation may be accelerated as a mechanism to reduce labor costs [2]. In high-volume kitchen subsegments, the integration of specialized cash protection systems is altering how workers accept payment from customers and balance receipts in cash registers [7]. For a specific organization in the United Kingdom, the task of serving food, beverages, or desserts has shifted from overseeing self-service cabinets back to manual retrieval from behind theft-proof counters to mitigate shoplifting [9]. In organization-specific deployments, the use of drone delivery is altering the final phase of delivering orders to customers [10], while AI assistants are beginning to handle the coordination of complex group orders [11]. A professional discourse has emerged regarding whether the prioritization of operational efficiency is eroding the empathy required when workers communicate with customers regarding orders, comments, and complaints [1]. Because this is primarily a critique of industry trends, the near-term effect is likely limited to shifts in performance evaluation criteria rather than operational mandates [1]. Tasks involving performing cleaning duties and preparing daily food items are unlikely to change because they require physical dexterity and strict adherence to sanitary measures [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, the occupation sees a targeted reduction in human voice-interaction tasks within drive-thru and phone-ordering subsegments and a broader shift in digital ordering interfaces, while high-volume settings adopt more rigid cash-handling protocols.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For workers in drive-thru and phone-ordering subsegments, if current trajectories of voice automation hold, the human role may shift from primary data entry to managing system exceptions and error resolution for requesting and recording customer orders [3][4][5][8]. Extrapolating from current discourse on efficiency and the proliferation of digital interfaces, the task of communicating with customers regarding complaints could become the primary human-facing responsibility as routine transactions are decoupled from human labor [1][6]. In high-wage regions, this transition may be more pronounced if financial pressures continue to drive the replacement of entry-level transactional roles [2]. The requirement to clean and organize eating, service, and kitchen areas will likely persist unchanged due to the high variability of physical debris and the necessity of human oversight for food safety compliance [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the subsegment of drive-thru and phone-ordering workers may transition into a role focused on service recovery and system oversight, while routine order-taking is handled by automated interfaces.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For workers in automated fast-service settings, the long-term structure of the role depends on whether the market values hospitality as a technical output or a uniquely human service [1]. One plausible outcome is that the human role is reduced primarily to embodied tasks, such as scrubbing and polishing counters, as simulated empathy in AI satisfies basic customer needs for routine transactions [1][3][4][5][8]. A competing outcome suggests that as automation becomes ubiquitous, human interaction may be re-established as a premium service layer for specific customer segments. It remains unknown whether regulatory bodies will mandate human oversight for specific customer-facing tasks to prevent systemic AI failure. High-level safety and regulatory oversight of food production will likely resist full automation due to the legal necessity of human accountability for food-borne illness [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the human role in fast-service settings may be reduced primarily to physical maintenance and sanitation tasks as the transactional and communicative elements of the occupation are fully automated.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation may bifurcate into a low-cost automated tier and a premium human-centric tier where interpersonal communication and empathy are marketed as luxury service attributes.*

title: Baristas
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For baristas in large-scale corporate coffee organizations, compensation structures may shift to include performance bonuses tied to store-level metrics [1][2]. This mechanism alters the incentive profile for the task to prepare or serve hot or cold beverages, as throughput speed and efficiency may now directly influence variable earnings [2]. These systems likely rely on point-of-sale data generated when workers receive and process customer payments to track performance [2]. Simultaneously, the adoption of these metrics may be contested or modified through collective bargaining and union organizing, which seek to influence workplace rules and compensation [3]. Such incentives may lead to a prioritization of speed over the time spent to describe menu items to customers [2]. However, the requirement to clean or sanitize work areas is unlikely to change, as it is governed by static health and safety regulations [4].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, baristas in specific high-volume corporate settings may experience a transition toward variable, metric-driven compensation models that are subject to labor negotiation.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For baristas in large-scale corporate coffee environments, if current trajectories hold, metric-linked incentive structures may propagate to other organizations with similar digital infrastructure for real-time monitoring [1][2]. The extent of this diffusion may be constrained by the success of labor organizing efforts that prioritize fixed wages over variable performance bonuses [3]. Independent cafes are unlikely to adopt these specific models because they lack the standardized data pipelines and prioritize different customer interaction markers than corporate chains [4]. Routine embodied tasks, such as stock customer service stations with paper products, will likely persist unchanged due to their low complexity and lack of a measurable speed-based benefit to the organization [4].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, metric-linked bonuses may become a contested standard for labor attraction and retention among large corporate coffee operators.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For workers in large-scale corporate coffee environments, one possibility involves the integration of sensor-based monitoring to automate the tracking of tasks like prepare or serve hot or cold beverages for real-time, algorithmic pay calculations [1][2]. A rival outcome is that labor regulations or collective bargaining agreements may prohibit variable pay tied to speed to prevent worker burnout, reverting compensation to fixed hourly rates [3]. It remains unknown whether the technical nuance of specialty beverage preparation will be fully automated or remain a human-led craft. Regardless of the compensation model, the requirement to take out garbage will likely resist change due to the high variability of the physical environment and the low incentive for automation [4].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, large organizations may implement high-precision automated monitoring to tightly couple compensation with per-second task efficiency.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, regulatory interventions or labor contracts may decouple wages from performance metrics to protect worker well-being in high-volume settings.*

title: Waiters and Waitresses
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For waiters and waitresses broadly, an emerging professional discourse suggests that the prioritization of operational efficiency may be eroding the empathetic quality of guest interactions [1]. This shift makes the task of taking orders from patrons for food or beverages more transactional, potentially reducing the interpersonal depth of the service [1]. Concurrently, reported consumer tipping fatigue may reduce the financial incentive for workers to perform high-empathy tasks, such as checking with customers to ensure they are enjoying their meals [2]. For servers in the United States, updated federal tax deduction rules regarding tips may alter the administrative overhead associated with the task of collecting payments from customers [3]. In metropolitan regions phasing out tip credits, as reported in Chicago, the shift toward higher base wages may decouple a worker's primary income from the immediate success of guest interactions [4][5]. For a subset of organizations adopting AI-powered ordering platforms, these tools may assume the role of "menu navigator," reducing the server's involvement in presenting menus to patrons and answering questions about menu items [6]. The task of removing dishes and glasses from tables is unlikely to change in this horizon because the capital cost of deploying robotics capable of navigating unstructured dining environments remains high relative to manual labor costs [7].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, the role may shift toward a more transactional function as efficiency-driven workflows, declining tipping incentives, and targeted AI adoption diminish the emphasis on high-touch hospitality.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For waiters and waitresses broadly, if current trajectories toward tipping volatility and transactional efficiency hold, the occupation may bifurcate based on the priced value of empathy. Extrapolating from the tension between efficiency and hospitality [1], low-cost dining segments may further automate the tasks of presenting menus and recording orders to reduce labor costs [6]. In contrast, high-end establishments may explicitly price human hospitality as a premium service to insulate worker income from volatile consumer tipping behavior [2]. The requirement to check patrons' identification to ensure they meet minimum age requirements for alcohol consumption will likely persist as a human-mediated task to manage legal liability and regulatory compliance [7].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupation may split into low-cost transactional roles focused on logistics and high-touch roles where empathy is treated as a priced luxury.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For waiters and waitresses broadly, the persistence of human staffing depends on the cost-convergence of humanoid robotics for embodied tasks. One plausible outcome is a systemic reduction in human presence where workers only intervene to correct any problems or handle complex social exceptions that automation cannot resolve [7]. A rival outcome is a market-driven resurgence in human-centric service as a reaction against total automation, where the hospitality factor [1] is restored as the primary value proposition of the dining experience. It remains unknown whether robotics will achieve the necessary site variability to reliably handle the task of cleaning tables or counters across diverse and changing restaurant layouts [7].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, human servers may be relegated to exception handlers who manage only the failures of an otherwise automated transactional system.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, a market correction may drive a resurgence in human-led hospitality, repositioning the server as a specialist in emotional labor.*

title: Food Servers, Nonrestaurant
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subset of workers in Chicago, the compensation structure is shifting as the city continues the phase-out of the tip credit [1]. This regulatory change requires employers to increase the base hourly wage rather than using tips to offset the minimum wage [1]. Because this shift is purely financial, the physical execution of core tasks, such as carrying food on trays [2] and loading trays with accessories [2], remains unchanged. Similarly, the clinical requirement to monitor food distribution for special diets [2] is unaffected by wage regulations, as these are governed by health and safety protocols rather than labor costs. It is unlikely that the basic sequence of taking food orders and relaying them to kitchens [2] will change in this horizon, as the regulatory signal does not introduce new delivery technologies.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, food servers in nonrestaurant settings in Chicago will experience a gradual increase in base wages as the tip credit is phased out.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For food servers in nonrestaurant settings in Chicago, if current regulatory trajectories hold, the complete removal of the tip credit may lead organizations to adjust staffing levels to offset higher fixed labor costs. Extrapolating from the wage shift, employers may seek to consolidate tasks, potentially requiring workers to spend more time recording amounts and types of special food items served [2] to increase administrative efficiency. However, the task of helping patients or patrons get situated for their meals [2] will likely persist unchanged due to the high demand for physical assistance in residential care and hospital settings.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the total elimination of tip credits in Chicago may drive organizations to consolidate service tasks to maintain margins.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For food servers in nonrestaurant settings in Chicago, the long-term outcome of the tip credit phase-out remains uncertain and depends on whether other jurisdictions adopt similar mandates. One plausible outcome is a standardized professional wage for nonrestaurant servers that removes the volatility of tip-based income. A rival outcome is that higher labor costs accelerate the adoption of automated delivery carts for the task of carrying food and linen [2], reducing the total number of human servers required per facility. It remains unknown whether the legal framework for "tipped employees" will survive as a category in institutional settings. Despite these shifts, the requirement to examine trays to ensure they contain required items [2] for medical or dietary compliance will likely resist full automation due to the high error cost of dietary mistakes.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation in Chicago evolves into a standardized wage-labor role with minimal reliance on gratuities.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the increased cost of human labor in Chicago leads to the replacement of the carry-and-delivery task with automated systems in large-scale institutional settings.*

title: Janitors and Cleaners, Except Maids and Housekeeping Cleaners
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For janitors and cleaners in commercial settings broadly, the introduction of intelligent scrubber and sweeper robots may alter the execution of cleaning building floors by sweeping, mopping, scrubbing, or vacuuming [1][2]. These autonomous systems reduce the manual labor required for large-area floor maintenance by automating repetitive navigation and scrubbing patterns [1]. The deployment of such equipment typically targets open-plan commercial environments where obstacles are predictable [1]. It is unlikely that the task of servicing, cleaning, or supplying restrooms will change significantly in this period because the highly unstructured nature of restroom interiors and the complexity of sanitizing vertical surfaces resist current robotic capabilities [2]. The worker's role may shift toward the basic operation and deployment of these units [1].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, automated floor cleaning tools may be adopted as supplementary equipment for high-traffic commercial areas.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For janitors and cleaners in commercial settings, if current trajectories in service robotics hold, automation may begin to touch the task of gathering and emptying trash [1][2]. This assumes that the delivery and collection mechanisms observed in early commercial service robots can be adapted for waste removal in standardized indoor environments [1]. Such a shift would require the deployment of standardized waste receptacles compatible with robotic interfaces. However, the task of making adjustments or minor repairs to heating, cooling, ventilating, plumbing, or electrical systems is likely to remain manual due to the high degree of dexterity and non-routine problem solving required [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupation may involve a higher proportion of equipment oversight and fleet management for workers in large-scale facilities.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For janitors and cleaners in commercial settings, the extent of further automation remains unknown, specifically regarding whether robotic systems can move beyond floors to handle dusting furniture, walls, machines, or equipment [2]. A primary uncertainty is whether general-purpose manipulation can reach a cost-performance parity with manual labor for complex surface cleaning. Despite these possibilities, the task of monitoring building security and safety by performing checks on electrical appliance use may resist full automation because it requires situational judgment and an understanding of building-specific hazards [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, a subset of core cleaning tasks in standardized commercial environments may be primarily handled by autonomous systems.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the inherent variability of building interiors and the lower cost of manual labor may limit robotics to a specialized niche of floor maintenance.*

title: Maids and Housekeeping Cleaners
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For housekeeping workers in commercial settings broadly, the deployment of intelligent scrubber and sweeper robots may automate specific floor-maintenance duties [1]. This technology targets the tasks of cleaning hallways, lobbies, and corridors and sweeping or scrubbing floors [2]. Because these robots operate on flat, open surfaces, they reduce the manual labor required for large-scale area maintenance [1]. However, tasks requiring high dexterity and the manipulation of soft materials, such as making beds or replenishing linens, are unlikely to change in the near term due to the mechanical complexity of textile handling [2]. The integration of such tools remains limited to the physical act of surface cleaning rather than the organizational management of a room [1].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, commercial housekeeping may see the partial automation of floor-cleaning tasks in large, open areas.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For housekeeping workers in commercial settings, if current trajectories in robotic scrubbing and sweeping hold, the worker's role may shift from performing these tasks to supervising the robots' deployment [1]. This transition could alter the task of cleaning rooms and hallways by moving the human worker into a monitoring and quality-assurance role [2]. Extrapolating from current commercial robot capabilities, workers may spend more time on task-switching and coordinating robot paths rather than manual scrubbing [1]. Tasks involving the disinfection of specialized equipment using germicides are likely to persist as human-led activities because of the variable precision required for medical-grade sanitation [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the role of commercial cleaners may shift toward supervising automated cleaning systems for floor-level maintenance.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For housekeeping workers in commercial settings, the extent of automation may depend on whether robotic dexterity reaches the threshold required for complex object manipulation. One plausible outcome is that all floor-level and hallway maintenance is fully handled by autonomous systems, leaving humans to focus exclusively on high-touch detail work [1]. A competing outcome is that the occupation bifurcates into a low-skill robot-tending role and a high-skill specialized cleaning role for luxury environments where human attention is a valued service component. It remains unknown whether battery technology and navigation sensors will ever allow for the seamless cleaning of highly cluttered, unstructured private household environments. Tasks such as cleaning rugs, carpets, and upholstered furniture may resist full automation due to the high variability in fabric types and fragility [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, floor-level cleaning in commercial settings may be almost entirely automated.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation may bifurcate into low-skill robot oversight and high-skill specialized cleaning for luxury or high-touch environments.*

title: Landscaping and Groundskeeping Workers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For landscaping and groundskeeping workers broadly, the adoption of effective robotic mowers may reduce manual labor hours spent to mow or edge lawns [1]. For a subset of workers providing pool maintenance, autonomous cleaners [2] and solar-powered surface skimmers [3] may reduce the frequency of manual debris removal. Because these systems automate the operation of powered equipment for turf and surface cleaning [1][3], the repetitive physical demand of these specific tasks decreases. This shift is likely concentrated in settings with predictable navigation and low obstacle density. The task to plant seeds, bulbs, foliage, or shrubs [4] is unlikely to change yet because the fine motor skills and site-specific judgment required for planting in unstructured soil exceed current robotic capabilities.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, automation may reduce manual labor hours for routine turf maintenance and surface pool cleaning.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For landscaping and groundskeeping workers broadly, if current trajectories in robotic turf maintenance hold, labor allocation may shift away from basic mowing [1]. For the subsegment of workers providing pool care, the reduction in manual skimming [3] may shift their focus toward more complex technical tasks such as maintaining irrigation systems [4]. As the requirement to operate vehicles or powered equipment for basic mowing declines, workers may spend a greater proportion of their time to prune or trim trees, shrubs, or hedges [4], which require higher precision and vertical reach. The task to gather and remove litter [4] persists unchanged due to the high variability of debris types and the unpredictable nature of litter placement in outdoor environments.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupation may shift toward a specialty role where routine maintenance is automated, increasing the relative proportion of pruning and system repair tasks.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For landscaping and groundskeeping workers broadly, long-term outcomes depend on whether robotic systems evolve into multi-purpose land managers. In one outcome, workers may transition to overseeing fleets of autonomous equipment while focusing on the high-aesthetic task to decorate gardens with stones or plants [4]. In a rival outcome, a shift toward ecological restoration and biodiversity mandates may render autonomous mowing less relevant, prioritizing manual soil and habitat management. It remains unknown whether sensors can reliably distinguish between invasive species and desired ground covers in complex, non-standardized landscapes. The task to shovel snow from walks and driveways [4] resists change because of the extreme variability of snow accumulation and the high torque required for clearance.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may transition into a fleet-management and high-end aesthetic design role.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation may pivot toward ecological land management and restoration, emphasizing manual biodiversity interventions over automated maintenance.*

title: Animal Caretakers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subset of workers in the pet care subsegment, specifically those providing exercise services, the deployment of quadruped robotic systems may begin to automate the task of exercising animals to maintain their physical and mental health [1]. Because these robotic platforms can navigate outdoor terrain and maintain a consistent pace, they could potentially replace the physical act of leading a dog on a walk [1]. This shift is likely limited to routine exercise tasks and does not extend to the broader occupation of animal caretaking in zoos or aquariums. Tasks requiring high tactile precision or clinical judgment, such as performing animal grooming duties or providing treatment to sick or injured animals, are unlikely to change because they require fine motor skills and sensory feedback that current robotic systems lack [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, robotic systems may be adopted by a small subset of pet care providers to automate routine exercise tasks.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For the same subset of workers in pet care, if current trajectories in robotic mobility and autonomy hold, the role may shift from performing the exercise task to overseeing the operation of robotic exercise systems. Extrapolating from current deployments, the human worker might instead focus on the task of examining and observing animals to detect signs of illness or injury before and after robotic-led exercise [1][2]. This transition remains conditional on the ability of robots to handle unpredictable animal behaviors safely. The task of responding to questions from patrons about animal behavior is likely to persist unchanged because it requires social perceptiveness and the ability to communicate nuance to human clients [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, a subset of pet care workers may transition from physical exercise providers to supervisors of robotic exercise systems.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For workers in the pet care subsegment, the long-term trajectory depends on whether robotic exercise is viewed as a functional utility or a deficiency in care. One possible outcome is the full integration of robotic exercise as a standard operational component in commercial kennels, provided that the psychological impact of robotic interaction on animals is found to be neutral or positive. A rival outcome is a market divergence where "human-led" exercise becomes a premium service, resisting automation due to the perceived value of human-animal bonding. It remains unknown whether robotic sensors will ever achieve the qualitative diagnostic capability required to observe animals for subtle signs of distress [2]. The task of cleaning and disinfecting animal quarters is likely to resist the specific robotic mechanisms used for dog walking due to the different environmental constraints of sanitation work [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, robotic exercise may become a standardized utility within the professional pet care subsegment.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, human-led exercise may be repositioned as a premium, non-automated service to differentiate care quality.*

title: Gambling Dealers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

In regions where U.S. tax regulations apply, the expansion of tip deduction rules may alter how dealers manage the administrative aspects of their compensation [1]. This change specifically affects tasks involving paying winnings or collecting bets [1] and the recording of patrons' cash wagers [1], as dealers must now account for digital payments and automatic gratuities under clarified IRS guidelines [1]. Because these regulations focus on the tax treatment of gratuities, the administrative burden of tracking these payments may increase for the worker [1]. The physical act of dealing cards to players (Task 7) is unlikely to change in this period because the tactile and social nature of live gaming remains the primary value proposition for casino patrons.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, dealers in the U.S. will experience a shift in how they document and report digital gratuities due to updated tax deduction frameworks.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

In regions with similar tax regimes to the U.S., if current trajectories toward digital payment formalization hold, the process of recording patrons' cash wagers (Task 9) may become increasingly integrated with automated tax-reporting systems [1]. This transition could reduce the manual effort required for dealers to track eligible tips for deduction purposes [1]. The necessity of greeting customers and making them feel welcome (Task 2) will likely persist, as the social-emotional labor of the role is a non-computable element of the gaming experience.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the administrative tracking of tips for dealers in these regions may shift from manual recording to automated, tax-compliant digital systems.*

## Far (2046–2051)

In regions where digital gratuity tracking has been standardized, the long-term impact of tax-integrated payment systems remains uncertain. One possibility is that the recording of winnings and losses (Task 13) becomes entirely decoupled from the dealer's manual input, handled instead by embedded table sensors and direct-to-tax digital ledgers [1]. A rival outcome is that increased regulatory scrutiny of digital tips leads to more rigid, audited reporting requirements that constrain how dealers interact with patrons during the exchange of currency (Task 3). Regardless of the reporting mechanism, the requirement to inspect cards and equipment for condition (Task 5) will likely resist change to ensure game integrity and prevent fraud.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, tip and wager reporting for dealers in these regions may become an invisible, fully automated background process integrated into the gaming table infrastructure.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the formalization of digital gratuities may lead to highly restrictive regulatory protocols that diminish the dealer's autonomy in managing table-side currency exchanges.*

title: Makeup Artists, Theatrical and Performance
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For makeup artists in major national media production hubs, technical proficiency in addressing specific skin and hair phenotypes is undergoing a standards update. Training initiatives, such as the 'Textured Hair & Make-up for Deep Skin-Tones Accelerator' in the United Kingdom, target the tasks of selecting and mixing makeup shades [1] and assessing skin types to ensure safety and efficacy [2]. This mechanism shifts the required competency for mixing oil, grease, and coloring from general color theory to phenotype-specific chemistry [2]. Such initiatives may alter how artists document specific looks and products on makeup sheets to ensure continuity across diverse casts [2]. The task of analyzing a script to determine character appearance remains unlikely to change, as it depends on narrative requirements and director intent rather than technical application standards [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, technical standards for makeup application in high-production media hubs will shift toward required proficiency in textured hair and deep skin tones.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For makeup artists in similar high-production environments, if current training trajectories hold, the mixing of specific color effects may move from an intuitive craft toward a standardized technical protocol based on evidence-driven skin-tone mapping [1]. This progression could refine the way artists examine photographs and models to obtain desired character images, requiring more precise color-matching data [2]. The use of specialized cosmetics for diverse skin tones may become a standard part of the requisition process for materials [2]. However, the physical requirement to alter or maintain makeup during productions to compensate for lighting changes will persist due to the unpredictable nature of physical lighting environments [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, phenotype-specific application standards may become a core component of professional competency benchmarks in major media hubs.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For makeup artists in high-production environments, the long-term impact of these technical standards remains uncertain due to the potential for high-fidelity digital skin replacement in post-production. One plausible outcome is that the requirement for physical precision in mixing colors becomes even more acute for productions that prioritize practical effects over digital augmentation [1]. A rival outcome is that these physical standards are marginalized as digital tools handle the majority of color and texture correction on performers [2]. The need to confer with performers to determine desired effects will likely resist change, as this task involves interpersonal negotiation and artistic interpretation that resists technical standardization [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, extreme technical specialization in skin-tone chemistry becomes a distinct professional sub-credential for practical-effects specialists in media hubs.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, physical skin-tone standards lose relevance as digital post-production handles the majority of color and texture correction.*

title: First-Line Supervisors of Retail Sales Workers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

In organizations utilizing AI agents for store management, the scope of supervisory work may shift toward managing the interface between automated systems and human staff. These agents may begin to automate symbolic tasks such as inventorying stock and reordering when levels drop [2] or planning and preparing work schedules [2]. However, early deployments indicate that agents may struggle with the interpersonal requirements of directing and supervising employees [2], specifically regarding the consistency of staff coordination and memory of personnel needs [1]. Consequently, the human supervisor's role in these specific settings may move toward correcting agent-driven scheduling or coordination errors [1]. Instructing staff on how to handle difficult and complicated sales [2] is unlikely to change in the near term because it requires high-order social perceptiveness and real-time nuance that current agent deployments lack.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, supervisors in organizations adopting management agents will see a reduction in symbolic administrative tasks but an increase in the need to mediate conflicts between automated agent directives and human staff requirements.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

In organizations employing advanced management agents, if current trajectories hold, the division of labor may bifurcate between "logistical supervision" and "personnel supervision." Agents may manage the majority of tasks related to reviewing inventory and sales records to prepare reports [2] and examining merchandise for correct pricing [2]. The human supervisor may be relegated to the purely interpersonal aspects of the role, such as evaluating personnel [2] or responding to complex customer complaints [2]. Enforcing safety, health, and security rules [2] likely persists as a human-led activity due to the requirement for physical presence and legal accountability for workplace safety.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, for a subset of supervisors in AI-integrated stores, the role may shift from general coordination to a specialized focus on human performance and emotional labor management.*

## Far (2046–2051)

In stores utilizing mature management agents, the extent of human supervisory necessity remains unknown, depending on whether agents can resolve the failure to maintain stable human staff relations seen in early deployments [1]. One possibility is that agents achieve bounded autonomy over all symbolic and logistical tasks, including estimating consumer demand [2] and formulating pricing policies [2], leaving the human supervisor as a purely cultural or brand ambassador. A rival outcome is that the friction between agent-driven efficiency and human staff retention leads some organizations to revert to human-centric lean management to avoid the personnel volatility associated with algorithmic supervision [1]. Providing customer service by greeting and assisting customers [2] in high-touch environments will likely resist total automation due to the continued value of human social signaling.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, for supervisors in highly automated settings, the role may evolve into a personnel coach who manages human staff's psychological well-being while the agent handles all operational logic.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the failures of agent-based personnel management may lead to a resurgence of traditional human supervisors who prioritize staff stability over algorithmic optimization.*


## References

title: Cashiers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

In retail organizations deploying agentic AI assistants and training employees on AI tools, the scope of the cashier's role may narrow as automated systems handle routine information retrieval. Because these tools can provide immediate answers regarding store policies and POS operations [1][2], the frequency with which cashiers must answer customers' questions and provide information on procedures or policies (O*NET Task 8) may decrease. This mechanism shifts the cashier's function from a primary knowledge source to a facilitator of AI-driven responses. Consequently, the time spent assisting customers by providing information and resolving complaints (O*NET Task 4) could be reduced for routine inquiries [2]. However, tasks involving physical manipulation, such as bagging, boxing, or wrapping merchandise (O*NET Task 26), are unlikely to change in these settings as the current deployments are software-based and lack the physical embodiment required for material handling.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, a subset of cashiers in organizations using agentic AI tools may experience a reduction in the cognitive load associated with routine procedural inquiries.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For cashiers in AI-enabled retail environments, if current trajectories hold, the use of agentic tools for transaction troubleshooting and policy guidance may move from experimental deployment to a standardized operational layer [1][2]. This could lead to a further atrophy of the need for cashiers to manually tabulate bills or identify prices of goods (O*NET Task 6) if AI assistants automate the validation and correction of pricing errors in real-time. Despite this, the requirement to maintain clean and orderly checkout areas and complete general cleaning duties (O*NET Task 12) persists, as AI software cannot perform the physical site hygiene required for retail operations.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the role of cashiers in AI-integrated organizations may shift further toward physical facility maintenance and the oversight of automated transaction flows.*

## Far (2046–2051)

In the subsegment of retail environments utilizing integrated agentic AI, the trajectory of the occupation remains uncertain due to the tension between automation efficiency and the error costs of financial disputes. One plausible outcome is that the task of resolving complaints (O*NET Task 4) is almost entirely handled by AI, leaving the human worker to focus primarily on physical security and inventory management. A rival outcome is that high-friction payment errors or complex returns (O*NET Task 11) create a renewed demand for human-centric validation to prevent customer churn. It remains unknown whether customers will accept fully automated dispute resolution for high-value transactions. The task of greeting customers entering establishments (O*NET Task 2) may resist change even at this horizon, provided that social norms continue to prioritize human interaction during the initial point of entry in physical commerce.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, cashiers in AI-integrated environments may evolve into physical site stewards whose primary function is security and inventory management.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, cashiers in these environments may see a resurgence in the importance of social perceptiveness as AI handles all routine tasks, leaving only high-emotion conflict resolution to the human worker.*

title: Retail Salespersons
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For retail salespersons broadly, the deployment of AI-driven interfaces may shift initial customer interactions toward automated systems [1]. In organizations using digital concierge interfaces, automated systems may now perform the task of greeting customers and ascertaining needs [2]. For retail salespersons in the beauty subsegment, AI assistants may automate the task of recommending and locating merchandise [3][4]. In organizations implementing AI phone agents for field store calls, as reported in the case of Home Depot, the task of answering questions regarding the store and its merchandise may be partially shifted from human staff to automated voice systems [5]. In large-scale retail organizations, the introduction of agentic AI tools may alter the daily workflow of employees as they are trained to interact with these systems to improve customer experience [6]. The task of cleaning shelves, counters, and tables is unlikely to change in the near term because there is no widely deployed robotic equivalent for these low-complexity manual tasks [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, initial customer greeting, basic product discovery, and routine store inquiries may shift from human associates to AI-driven digital and voice interfaces.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For retail salespersons broadly, if current trajectories hold, the worker's role may transition from being the primary source of product knowledge to acting as a validator of AI-generated recommendations. Extrapolating from the use of digital concierges and agentic commerce [2][4], the task of recommending and selecting merchandise may shift toward refining and confirming options already presented to the customer by an AI [1]. Human associates may focus more on the task of preparing merchandise for purchase, which remains a physical labor requirement [2]. The core responsibility to watch for and recognize security risks is likely to persist unchanged because physical theft prevention requires real-time human judgment and situational awareness of the physical store environment [1].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupation may move toward a hybrid model where AI manages data-driven product discovery and routine inquiries while humans manage physical fulfillment and store security.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For retail salespersons broadly, the long-term structure of the occupation depends on the potential integration of embodied robotics on the sales floor. One rival outcome is that high-value retail remains a human-centric experience to maintain a luxury brand signal, while budget retail becomes largely automated. A significant uncertainty remains whether AI-integrated robotics can eventually perform the task of inventorying stock and requisitioning new stock without human oversight [1]. Even at this horizon, the task of exchanging merchandise and accepting returns may resist full automation because of the complex social negotiation and emotional labor required to resolve customer disputes [1].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may bifurcate into high-touch specialized consultation for luxury goods and low-touch logistics management for automated stores.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, widespread adoption of embodied robotics may automate both the information and the physical handling tasks, reducing the human role to a minimal supervisory presence.*

title: Advertising Sales Agents
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subset of advertising sales agents selling on AI-native or agentic-enabled platforms, the adoption of dedicated ads manager tools may automate providing clients with estimates of costs [3] and processing paperwork related to accounts [8] [1]. The deployment of agentic ads—advertisements that function as interactive chatbots—shifts the value proposition from static impressions to automated lead generation, altering how agents explain to customers how specific advertising helps promote products [5] and how they recommend appropriate formats [12] [2]. Because these tools standardize AI-native placements, the mechanism for preparing promotional plans and sales literature [7] shifts from manual document creation to platform-driven configuration [1]. However, the delivery of sales presentations to new and existing customers [1] is unlikely to change, as the acquisition of high-spend accounts still requires interpersonal persuasion and high-context negotiation.

*Hypothesis: For a subset of agents selling on AI-enabled platforms, administrative tasks will be partially automated while the sales value proposition shifts from impression-based to interaction-based in the near term.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For the same subset of workers in AI-platform sales, if current trajectories hold, the task of obtaining and studying information about clients' products and needs [6] may evolve into configuring the behavioral parameters and knowledge bases of agentic ad bots [2]. The mechanism for preparing sample advertisements within a selected medium [14] could shift from visual layout and copy [13] to the design of conversational workflows and interaction scripts [2]. Despite these shifts, consulting with company officials and advertising agencies to develop promotional plans [16] will likely persist as a human-led task due to the requirement for cross-departmental organizational alignment and strategic nuance.

*Hypothesis: For a subset of agents in AI-platform sales, the role may shift from selling ad space to designing and optimizing interactive AI-driven lead generation flows in the mid term.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For the subset of agents specializing in agentic media, the role may diverge based on the evolution of B2B procurement. In one scenario, the agent evolves into a high-level consultant who manages a fleet of AI tools to develop promotional plans [16], while the tactical execution of determining the advertising medium [14] becomes entirely autonomous. In a competing scenario, the requirement for a human agent to study client needs [6] may be superseded by AI-to-AI negotiation between an advertiser's procurement system and the platform's ads manager [1]. It remains unknown whether the ads manager will continue to function as a tool for the agent or evolve into a replacement for the transactional agent. The final legal approval of contracts [9] is likely to resist full automation due to the necessity of human accountability in high-value corporate agreements.

*Hypothesis A: For a subset of agents in AI-platform sales, the role evolves into high-level strategic consultancy focused on organizational alignment in the far term.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): For a subset of agents in AI-platform sales, the role is eliminated as AI-to-AI procurement systems automate the entire lifecycle from lead generation to contract approval in the far term.*

title: Insurance Sales Agents
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For agents in the brokerage subsegment, administrative friction remains a primary constraint on operational efficiency. The process of performing administrative tasks [4], specifically the assembly of new submissions, is hindered by fragmented data across emails and attachments [1]. This bottleneck slows the ability to contact underwriters and submit forms to obtain binder coverage [4] because agents must manually synthesize scattered client details [1]. Simultaneously, in regions where state-level licensing entry is streamlined, as observed in Pennsylvania, the workforce may expand more rapidly due to reduced barriers to entry [3]. In the brokerage subsegment, the mechanism for onboarding new agents is shifting from experiential shadowing to AI-supported execution, which standardizes the baseline quality of performance for new hires [2]. This transition alters how agents learn to explain features, advantages, and disadvantages of policies [4] by providing a structured floor for execution [2]. The requirement to interview prospective clients to obtain data about financial resources and physical conditions [4] is unlikely to change yet due to the high error cost associated with inaccurate risk assessment.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, brokerage agents will experience standardized, AI-supported onboarding while remaining constrained by manual data fragmentation, while some regions may see workforce growth through streamlined licensing.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For agents in the brokerage subsegment, if current trajectories toward AI-standardized execution and document orchestration hold, the mechanism of data ingestion may shift. Extrapolating from current bottlenecks in submission handling [1] and the adoption of tools that raise the execution floor [2], the task of maintaining records and handling policy renewals [4] could move from manual document assembly to the oversight of automated synthesis tools. This shift may reduce the time spent on the low-value administrative components of contacting underwriters [4]. However, the need to explain features, advantages, and disadvantages of various policies [4] will likely persist unchanged because this task relies on persuasion and social perceptiveness to align complex products with specific client needs [4], which exceeds the baseline execution floor [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the administrative burden of submission assembly for brokerage agents may decrease as automated data synthesis and standardized execution tools reduce manual document handling.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For agents in the brokerage subsegment, the long-term evolution of the submission process depends on whether data standardization occurs across the insurance ecosystem. One outcome is the total elimination of the submission bottleneck through real-time, standardized data exchange between clients and underwriters. A rival outcome is that administrative friction persists or increases because regulatory requirements for documentation become more granular and complex. The core task of coordinating between clients and underwriters to obtain coverage [4] will likely resist full automation due to the necessity of negotiating bespoke terms for non-standard risks. It remains unknown whether the brokerage model will survive if the friction of customizing insurance programs [4] is entirely removed.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, standardized data ecosystems eliminate the administrative bottleneck in brokerage submissions, shifting the agent's role almost entirely to risk advisory.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, increasing regulatory complexity maintains or increases the administrative burden of policy submissions despite advances in automation.*

title: Securities, Commodities, and Financial Services Sales Agents
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subset of workers in the mortgage lending subsegment, the adoption of AI pre-underwriting tools may shift the nature of initial client interactions [1]. As AI automates the verification of documents and initial risk assessments, the task of interviewing clients to determine assets and liabilities may shift from manual data collection to the validation of AI-generated summaries [2]. This transition moves the operational focus toward customer success roles that manage the output of these tools rather than performing the primary data review [1]. The task of reviewing transactions to ensure conformance to governing agency regulations is unlikely to change significantly in the near term because of the high error cost and legal liability associated with lending mandates [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, agents in the mortgage subsegment may see a shift in task allocation where AI manages initial risk data and humans focus on managing the client's experience through the automated pipeline.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For the same subset of mortgage-focused agents: if current trajectories hold, AI tools could expand from pre-underwriting to the preliminary generation of tailored loan proposals. This may alter the process of preparing proposals to sell services that address client needs by automating the matching of loan products to AI-verified financial profiles [2]. The core task of discussing financial options with clients will likely persist unchanged, as the high-stakes nature of home financing requires trust and nuanced negotiation to resolve client anxieties [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the role for mortgage-focused agents may transition toward a hybrid of customer success and final-stage negotiation, with AI handling the majority of the proposal construction.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For agents within the mortgage lending niche: the long-term trajectory depends on whether regulatory bodies permit autonomous final approvals. If autonomous systems are permitted, the role may transition entirely into a platform-management function where the agent oversees the interface between the client and the software [1]. Conversely, if liability laws continue to mandate a human signatory for all financial commitments, the agent's role may consolidate around final risk certification and high-level relationship management for complex cases [2]. It remains unknown whether AI can accurately model the idiosyncratic risk of non-standard borrowers. The requirement for a licensed professional to assume legal responsibility for financial advice is likely to resist change even at this horizon [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, mortgage sales agents in this subsegment may evolve into customer success managers for fully automated lending platforms.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the role may narrow into a specialized "risk certifier" role where the human agent provides the final legal sign-off on AI-generated loan approvals.*

title: Travel Agents
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For travel agents broadly, conversational AI interfaces may reduce the manual labor required for conversing with customers to determine destination and computing cost of travel [1][2]. By enabling travelers to search, compare, and book itineraries within a chat interface, these tools shift the initial discovery and pricing tasks from the agent to the consumer [1]. This mechanism potentially reduces the demand for agents who specialize in low-complexity, price-sensitive itineraries [1]. However, the task of providing customers with brochures and publications regarding specific foreign country regulations is unlikely to change significantly, as these often require nuanced, up-to-date legal interpretations and personalized guidance that generic AI may not reliably provide [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, conversational AI may automate the discovery and pricing phases of travel planning for a broad segment of consumers.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For travel agents broadly, if conversational booking interfaces become the primary consumer interface, the role may shift toward managing exceptions and high-complexity logistics. Extrapolating from the integration of trend dashboards and conversational planning [1], agents may move away from the routine task of booking transportation and hotel reservations for standard trips [2]. The necessity of recording and maintaining information on clients likely persists as a core human function to ensure personalized relationship management in an increasingly automated market [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, travel agents may transition from transactional booking providers to high-touch curation consultants as standard itinerary planning is commoditized.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For travel agents broadly, the professional viability of the role depends on whether the value proposition shifts entirely to luxury curation or to technical orchestration. One unresolved uncertainty is the degree to which carriers will open their proprietary booking systems to fully autonomous AI agents without human oversight. The core activity of collecting payment for transportation and accommodations may remain a high-friction point that resists full automation due to liability and fraud constraints [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may contract into a niche luxury service where human agents manage complex, high-value experiences that resist algorithmic standardization.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, travel agents may evolve into system orchestrators who manage a suite of autonomous AI tools to optimize travel for corporate or complex group clients.*
